report.executiveSummary:
Three habits change immediately. First, the words "landscape architect," "landscape architecture" and "landscape architectural" never appear in GMZ's marketing, proposals or design agreement: using them without that license is a misdemeanor with a fine up to $5,000, while "landscape design by a licensed landscape contractor" is safe. Second, every agreement signed at a client's kitchen table, design or construction, carries the statutory right-to-cancel notice, and because clients in Atherton, Hillsborough and Woodside often qualify as seniors, the five day version will often be the correct one; the clock runs from delivery of the signed copy containing the notice. Third, on any rebate job, no lawn comes out and no materials are bought until the client holds a written Notice to Proceed from their water supplier; starting early forfeits the rebate permanently.

Study 001 established that a licensed landscape contractor may sign the MWELO design plan but could not say how far the design authority reaches. Study 002 pulled the statutes verbatim. The authority comes from two parallel sections, one in the contractors' law and one in the landscape architects' law, and both tie it to work "to be performed and supervised by that contractor." The regulator's own reference document then says in writing that a C-27's design deliverables may include construction documents with specifications and details. So GMZ's paid design package can be construction ready, not concept only, which is exactly what separates it from what unlicensed garden designers may legally sell.

What no source of any tier resolves, still, is the design-only case: what happens when the client pays for design and never builds, or takes the plans to another builder. No case, Attorney General opinion or licensing board guidance addresses it. Whether the "performed and supervised" limit is judged by what the parties anticipated at signing or by what actually happened afterward is the single question GMZ most needs a California construction attorney to answer, and the counsel brief assembles everything needed to ask it in one visit.

Whether the standalone design agreement is itself a home improvement contract is also nowhere stated. The definitional chain, home improvement contract to home improvement services to services bought in connection with the improvement of real property, plausibly reaches a design fee. The safe and cheap answer is to draft the design agreement to comply with the home improvement contract rules anyway: include the cancellation notice, honor the cancel window, respect the deposit cap. Study 002 also added something new for the maintenance line: small ad hoc repairs can use the lighter service-and-repair contract form only when all four conditions hold, price $750 or less, the client called first, no selling beyond the presenting problem, and no money collected until the work is done.

Study 002 corrected the record as well as extending it. The largest correction: the home improvement contract statute was amended effective January 2026, which Study 001 missed; every provision GMZ relies on was re-verified in the current text, but counsel should still review what else the amendment changed. Smaller corrections came out of the audit: the C-27 regulation's wording, a Delaware fee bracket overstatement, and the famous "6 percent design fee," which turns out to be a narrow federal cap on producing drawings for public works, not a price for design.

On the design fee itself, the honest position is now well documented. No industry standard percentage exists in any source worth citing, and antitrust history explains why no association publishes one. What does exist is a consistent pattern in government fee schedules: the percentage rises as the project shrinks. Washington pays 10.65 percent for full design services on residence-class work at its smallest published size; Delaware pays up to 13 percent on small complex renovations; the Department of Defense just raised its cap from 6 to 10 percent; California's own highway program accepts pre-construction costs near 20 percent of construction. GMZ's 10 to 15 percent sits inside the published public band, and the stronger client argument is the one the federal government itself uses: qualified design is selected on qualifications, and the research suggests avoided construction cost growth dwarfs a few points of design fee.

The maintenance renewal escalator can now be drafted with real numbers. The 2027 minimum wage is certified at $17.40, a 2.99 percent step known before any fall renewal notice goes out. The local all-items index is running 3.8 percent while the gardening services index is running 12.3 percent, so the choice of index is the pricing decision. The clause must name the exact index series and a fallback, because the government skipped publishing a month during the 2025 shutdown, and it must reference an even month, because the local index prints only six times a year. The annual renewal notice, legally required 15 to 45 days before renewal on auto-renewing accounts, should state the computed new dollar amount rather than letting the formula run silently. Two executed public contracts, Los Gatos and Fairfield, supply tested clause language and one cautionary tale about naming an index that no longer exists.

Every permit, tree and rebate fact is strictly per town, and none transfers. A crew working three towns in one week can face three different tree regimes, three fence rules and three rebate programs on identical scopes. Study 002 captured verified rules for several towns, but many of the source pages are undated, Palo Alto's tree thresholds rest on a nonprofit summary because the city's own pages block automated retrieval, and a 2024 Palo Alto amendment of unknown effect is outstanding. The practical product is a per-town intake checklist, not a general rule.

On referrals, reviews and retention, the directions are solid and the magnitudes are borrowed from other industries. Referred customers are more valuable and more loyal, but the loyalty depends on the referrer staying a client, so the right people to ask are established, satisfied maintenance accounts, and keeping a referrer keeps two relationships. Retention effort has several times the value leverage of acquisition effort, which favors the recurring accounts. Review asks work best mentioning that other clients have left reviews, and never with payment, which the platforms prohibit. The 30-day and six-month call timing is practitioner convention; no study tests it.

What remains open, beyond the design-only question: local minimum wage ordinances in GMZ's towns, which likely exceed the state floor; business license rules in the nine towns besides Redwood City; MWELO status in every jurisdiction except Menlo Park; and Cal Water's rebate rate, which is not published anywhere public. Those are phone calls and account lookups, not research problems, and several of the remaining questions can only be settled by GMZ's own records.

themes.title: The C-27 design authority now stands on quoted text, and it reaches construction documents
themes.summary: Both B&P 7027.5 and B&P 5641.4 grant design authority in identical terms limited to work performed and supervised by that contractor, the C-27 regulation itself grants no design activity, the LATC's own reference states a C-27's deliverables may include construction documents with specifications and details, B&P 5641 confines unlicensed designers to conceptual work for single family dwellings, and B&P 5640 makes unlicensed use of the protected titles a misdemeanor. The frame is complete and verbatim; only the design-only edge case remains unresolved.
themes.whatItMeansForGmz: Sell the design step as a construction-ready deliverable, which unlicensed competitors cannot legally offer. Recite in the design agreement that the plans are prepared for work GMZ will perform and supervise. Ban the protected titles from every page and proposal. Take the design-only question to counsel before leaning harder on the two-agreement structure.

themes.title: Treat the design agreement as a home improvement contract until counsel says otherwise
themes.summary: No statute or guidance says whether a contractor's design-only agreement is a home improvement contract, but the definitional chain from 7151.2 through 7151 into Civil Code 1689.5 plausibly reaches a design fee. The cancellation-notice trigger in 7159(e)(6) is locational, CSLB's guidance blends in a $25 threshold from the Home Solicitation Sales Act, and the service-and-repair carve-out for small jobs has four strict conditions including no payment until completion. Advertising and license-number statutes close Study 001's two open items.
themes.whatItMeansForGmz: Drafting the design agreement to full 7159 compliance costs little and forecloses the classification argument. Include the right-to-cancel notice in both agreements signed at the client's home, defaulting to the five-day version for clients 65 and over. Use the service-and-repair form on maintenance-account repairs only when all four conditions hold, and never collect in advance on one.

themes.title: The fee percentage is defensible by government curves, not by an industry standard
themes.summary: No association publishes a design-fee benchmark, a fact consistent with the AIA antitrust decrees, and no tiered source states a residential landscape percentage. What exists instead is uniform: every published government fee schedule rises as project size falls, Washington's residence-class schedule starts at 10.65 percent at its smallest tabulated size, Delaware reaches 13 percent on small complex renovations, the folk 6 percent is a narrow federal drawings-production cap that Congress just raised to 10 percent for defense work, and Brooks Act policy selects design on qualifications with QBS research showing large avoided cost growth.
themes.whatItMeansForGmz: Never claim an industry standard exists. Present the fee as GMZ's price for a defined scope, contextualized by public fee schedules that are buyer publications, not seller price-fixing. Remember the honest comparison: GMZ sells design only, roughly two thirds of a full-service fee, on renovation-type sites smaller than any published curve reaches, both of which push the defensible percentage up, not down.

themes.title: The maintenance escalator can be drafted now, with the index named exactly
themes.summary: Every input is in hand: the certified 2027 wage step (+2.99 percent to $17.40), the statutory escalator formula worth copying (lesser-of cap, defined window, rounding, announcement date), current prints for the local all-items index (3.8 percent) versus the trade index (12.3 percent), local wage benchmarks, the automatic renewal law's 15-to-45-day notice and cancellation duties applying to every account as it rolls over after July 2025, and two executed public escalation clauses. The failure modes are documented too: a skipped publication month and a contract naming an index that no longer exists.
themes.whatItMeansForGmz: Peg to the SF metro all-items index by exact series ID, reference an even month, state a fallback for unpublished months, and make the adjustment upward-only with a floor as Los Gatos does. Because a plain cost-of-living escalator underruns this trade's cost curve, pair it with a floor or wage-step add-on. Send each year's computed dollar amount inside the required renewal notice window rather than applying the formula silently.

themes.title: Ten towns, ten rulebooks: permits, trees and rebates are strictly per jurisdiction
themes.summary: Verified town-level rules now exist for turf rebate rates and their Notice-to-Proceed sequencing, Menlo Park's local water ordinance with its designer audit duties, heritage tree definitions in Atherton and Menlo Park down to the inch, grading and retaining wall triggers, fence permit lines, and Redwood City's business license. But sources are frequently undated, Palo Alto rests on a nonprofit summary, and none of it transfers between towns.
themes.whatItMeansForGmz: Build a per-town intake checklist: incorporation status of the address, water supplier, tree survey against that town's thresholds, permit triggers for walls, fences and grading. Put tree and permit contingencies into the design agreement, where an Atherton heritage tree can add a month and $750 before construction pricing. Sequence every rebate job so the pre-inspection happens with the lawn still in place.

themes.title: Referrals and retention: the direction is proven, the magnitudes are borrowed
themes.summary: Peer-reviewed work shows referred customers are worth more and stay longer, that their loyalty collapses if their referrer leaves, that retention effort has several times the value leverage of acquisition effort, that reviews matter most for independent firms and unfamiliar buyers, and that norm-based review asks measurably work. Every study is banking, restaurants, platforms or e-commerce; nothing measures home services, and the follow-up call timing has no evidence at all.
themes.whatItMeansForGmz: Ask for referrals selectively: established maintenance accounts at least six months in, satisfied and unlikely to leave. Treat a lapsing referrer as two at-risk relationships. Steer referred design/build clients toward the maintenance book, where the loyalty advantage actually lives. At the follow-up call, mention that other clients have left reviews; never pay for one. Quote none of the borrowed percentages to clients.

productSummaries.title: GMZ Landscaping Inc., One-Visit Counsel Brief: Design Agreement, Home Improvement Contract Coverage, Cancellation Rights, Plan License, Maintenance Contracts
productSummaries.twoLineSummary: A brief for a California construction attorney assembling, with verbatim statutory text, every question Study 002 could frame but not close: whether the design-only agreement sits inside the C-27 design authority, whether it is a home improvement contract, which cancellation notice applies where, what license the client gets in a paid plan set, and how the maintenance contracts are classified. Built so counsel confirms or corrects each position in one sitting instead of researching from scratch.
openItems: Whether 'to be performed and supervised by that contractor' in B&P 7027.5/5641.4 is judged by anticipation at contracting or by outcome; no authority found either way
Whether a design-only agreement is a home improvement contract under the 7151.2/7151/CIV 1689.5 chain; the chain is assembled, not sourced
Full diff of SB 517's 2026 amendments to B&P 7159, including any changes to paragraph (7)'s Seven-Day Right to Cancel
DCA Legal Guide K-10 identified but not retrieved; may bear on the cancellation-trigger reconciliation
Whether the $750 in 7159.10 is measured per visit, per month, or per term for a recurring maintenance account
Whether a pre-agreed escalation formula is a 'material change' under B&P 17602 or whether stating the computed price in the annual notice suffices
CSLB guidance pages not yet updated against SB 517; their framing may be stale

productSummaries.title: Maintenance Renewal and Escalator Design
productSummaries.twoLineSummary: A drafting package for the annual price adjustment on the roughly 24 recurring accounts: an upward-only adjustment pegged to the SF metro all-items index named by exact series ID with an even-month reference and a published-index fallback, paired with a floor or wage-step add-on because the local index underruns this trade's costs. Delivery rides inside the legally required 15-to-45-day renewal notice, which states each year's computed dollar amount, with a worked example and the Los Gatos and Fairfield clauses as tested precedent.
openItems: Peninsula city minimum wage ordinances above the state floor were not researched; several GMZ towns may have their own, which would move the wage-step floor for crews working there.
Whether a pre-agreed escalation formula is a 'material change' under B&P 17602 is legally unsettled; the recommended annual dollar-amount notice sidesteps rather than resolves it.
The SF-Oakland-Hayward index excludes Santa Clara County, so Palo Alto and Los Altos accounts escalate on an index that does not technically cover them; no finer BLS index exists.
Exact add-on size, cap level, and rounding convention are business decisions, not research questions.
Year 2 of the worked example uses hypothetical CPI and wage-step values, since neither is published yet.
Treatment of any future commercial or HOA maintenance accounts, which sit outside the consumer automatic renewal law.

productSummaries.title: Water Rebate Sales Asset: Turf-Replacement Rebates Across GMZ's Ten Peninsula Towns
productSummaries.twoLineSummary: A town-by-town sheet mapping each of the ten service-area towns to its turf-replacement rebate route and published rate where one exists: BAWSCA agency rates in San Mateo County, Valley Water terms for Los Altos and Palo Alto addresses, and check-with-your-supplier flags where rates or boundaries are unverified. Its operational core is the sequencing rule every route shares: the client must hold a written Notice to Proceed before any lawn removal, so design-phase scheduling leaves the turf untouched.
openItems: Per-agency maximum caps for the San Mateo County (BAWSCA Lawn Be Gone!) agencies are not stated on the program page; each cap must be confirmed with the individual agency before a client conversation.
Whether Mid-Peninsula Water District ($4.00/sq ft) actually serves specific San Carlos and Belmont addresses was not verified from a primary source; supplier lookup by address is required.
Which of Atherton, Woodside and Portola Valley fall inside Cal Water's Bear Gulch district was not verified from a primary source, so those three towns are listed as check-with-your-supplier.

Cal Water's per-square-foot rebate rate is not published on its public page; it is only visible inside a customer Conservation Portal account, so no dollar figure can be quoted for Cal Water-served clients.

The BAWSCA Lawn Be Gone! page is undated and links documents referencing FY19-20 and FY20-21, so the listed rates ($2.00 Redwood City, $3.00 Menlo Park, $1.00 Hillsborough, $4.00 Mid-Peninsula WD) may lag the current fiscal year.

Whether the City of Palo Alto's municipal utility runs its own landscape rebate program in addition to the Valley Water program was not checked; only the Valley Water route is confirmed for Palo Alto addresses.
The 75 sq ft minimum conversion area sometimes reported for the Valley Water program does not appear on the main program page and remains unconfirmed.

gaps: No Attorney General opinion, CSLB newsletter article, or published disciplinary decision addressing a design-only agreement by a C-27 licensee was found; whether 7027.5/5641.4's 'work to be performed and supervised by that contractor' tolerates a paid design phase where the client never builds, or takes the plans to another builder, is unresolved in every primary and regulator text located. This is the single question GMZ most needs construction counsel to answer.

B&P 7159 needs a complete pull by counsel: it was amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 585 (SB 517), effective 2026-01-01, which the original research missed. The quoted (e)(6) trigger, notice text, senior five-day substitution and (a)(2) carve-out were re-verified in the current text, but the full scope of SB 517's changes was not diffed, paragraph (7)'s Seven-Day Right to Cancel was not read, and the statutory notice form's formatting requirements (type size, duplicate copies) were not extracted verbatim. CSLB's undated consumer guidance pages may predate the amendment.

Civil Code 1689.6 and 1689.7 (cancellation mechanics and notice form for home solicitation contracts) were not fetched; DCA Legal Guide K-10 (dca.ca.gov/publications/legal_guides/k_10.pdf) surfaced in search as the obvious next T1 pull for the cancellation reconciliation but was not fetched.

16 CCR 832.27 was read from CSLB's official classification page (re-verified in audit, including the Authority/Reference notes); the canonical govt.westlaw.com/calregs page was not fetched, so the Register history (filed 6-1-88, operative 7-1-88, Register 88, No. 23) rests on the Cornell LII reproduction.

B&P 5640.1, named in the task, does not appear to exist: leginfo returned no section text, and the Practice Act's exemption sections enumerate as 5640, 5641, 5641.1 through 5641.6, 5642 and 5644, consistent with the LATC Permitted Practices citations. The intended cite was probably 5640 or one of the 5641.x exemptions, all of which were fetched.
LATC's FAQ page (latc.ca.gov/consumers/faq.shtml) was never fetched; an earlier assertion that it repeats the C-27 design rule was removed in audit. Fetch it before citing it.

The LATC 'Permitted Practices in California' PDF is undated on its face (September 2023 per XMP metadata) and disclaims legal effect; no dated LATC enforcement action or meeting decision specifically construing the 5641.4 contractor exemption was located (committee minutes surfaced in search but were not fetched).

B&P 7027.1(b)'s full advertising-definition text was returned partially paraphrased by the verification fetch; the finding's quote was trimmed to verified phrases. Pull the full (b) text if the exact definition matters for the website review.

No T1 or T2 source addresses pricing of a contractor's design phase, and no tiered source states a design-fee percentage for residential landscape work specifically: every residential percentage found (5-20%, 10-20%, 6-15%) lives on rejected lead-generation or vendor sites with no disclosed method, confirming Study 001's folklore finding at a second attempt. The statutes read are silent on design fees, so GMZ's pricing model is a business choice, not a compliance question, on the texts located.

ASLA publishes no fee benchmark or fee survey with disclosed methodology that could be located; a trade-press claim about 'the latest ASLA business survey' could not be traced to any ASLA document with disclosed method and was discarded. The antitrust finding claims only consistency with, not causation of, this absence.

Palo Alto primary sources remain unreachable by automated fetch (paloalto.gov PDFs and the amlegal-hosted municipal code both returned 403), so Palo Alto tree findings rest on Canopy's nonprofit summary (T3). Palo Alto also adopted a further tree-ordinance amendment in 2024 (Ordinance 5612, per search results) whose effect on the 11.5/15/18-inch thresholds is unverified, and the widely repeated 'roughly tripled the number of protected trees' claim was removed because it does not appear on the cited source and describes the pre-2024 state. A human should pull current PAMC 8.10.020 before anything client-facing is written.

BAWSCA Lawn Be Gone page staleness: the fetched page is undated and links documents referencing FY19-20 and FY20-21; the researcher's claimed 'FY 2026-27 program year' reference could not be reproduced. Confirm current-year per-square-foot rates and any per-agency caps directly with each agency before quoting totals to clients.

The claim that artificial turf is ineligible for Lawn Be Gone (attributed to Mid-Peninsula WD) and that Mid-Peninsula WD serves Belmont and part of San Carlos were not verifiable on the fetched BAWSCA page; the page links an Artificial Turf Fact Sheet without an eligibility statement.

Atherton's Tree Removal Procedure handout is undated, so the $750 fee, 19-day lead and hearing schedule may have changed; the heritage-tree measurement height conflicts across sources (handout: 48 inches above grade; secondary summaries of current AMC 8.10.020: 54 inches). The code host was Cloudflare-blocked; confirm both with Atherton Planning.
Menlo Park heritage-tree root-pruning threshold: the cited city article confirms the 25% canopy trigger but says nothing about roots. Check Ch. 13.24 before relying on a root-work trigger.

MWELO implementation status (state model applied as-is vs local ordinance) was confirmed only for Menlo Park (local, Ch. 12.44). Redwood City, Atherton, Woodside, Portola Valley, San Carlos, Belmont, Hillsborough, Los Altos, Palo Alto and San Mateo County unincorporated remain unverified; the state model applies by default where no local ordinance was adopted, but which towns adopted stricter versions is unknown.

Cal Water's lawn-to-garden per-square-foot rebate rate is not published on its public conservation page (re-confirmed in audit); the rate for Bear Gulch and Mid-Peninsula district customers is unquantified, and Cal Water district boundaries within GMZ's towns were not verified from a primary source.
Valley Water's minimum conversion area (75 sq ft per a support article) does not appear on the main landscape-rebates page and remains unconfirmed.

Palo Alto rebate stacking (Valley Water Landscape Rebate plus BAWSCA Lawn Be Gone) is asserted only by local press; BAWSCA's participating-agency list does not include Palo Alto (re-confirmed), so treat stacking as unverified until CPAU or BAWSCA confirms it.

Business license / contractor registration requirements were verified only for Redwood City. Palo Alto, Menlo Park, Atherton, Woodside, Portola Valley, San Carlos, Belmont, Los Altos and Hillsborough were not checked; several Peninsula towns require a license of out-of-town contractors per job.
Tree ordinances for Woodside, Los Altos, Hillsborough, San Carlos, Belmont and Redwood City were not researched; only Atherton, Menlo Park, Palo Alto and (partially) Portola Valley are covered.

Portola Valley's exact Site Development Permit trigger (a 50-cubic-yard figure appears in secondary code summaries) was not verified on the fetched town page; only the 100/1,000 cy review tiers and fence rules were confirmed.

Fence height zoning limits (as opposed to building-permit exemptions) were not captured for most towns; Redwood City's R-district fence standards PDF and equivalents in Atherton, Hillsborough and Los Altos remain unread. Redwood City's Building FAQ references the 2019 California Codes, so its currency should be confirmed with the Building Division.

Impervious surface / maximum hardscape coverage limits, a known constraint in Woodside and Atherton zoning, were not located in a fetchable primary source; only Portola Valley's definition of impervious surfaces (including compacted gravel and rock areas) was captured.

General transferability note: all permit findings are per-jurisdiction and none transfer between towns; a small GMZ crew working three towns in a week can face three different tree, fence and grading regimes on otherwise identical scopes.

California publishes no state A/E percentage fee curve: DGS SAM 6828 returned 404, search summaries indicate DGS prices A&E work by detailed task analysis, and CSU's 'Determination of Fee' framework has proposers state their own percentages without publishing values. The nearest published state curves used here are Washington and Delaware.

The primary Chinowsky/Kingsley QBS study PDF could not be fetched (403 at acec.ca; the ACEC Research Institute portal gates it); its figures are carried via the 2018 QBS Canada/OAA report's page-cited summaries, which the audit verified. The 2009 study date is corroborated by ACEC-ecosystem search results only. If GMZ wants to quote the study directly, obtain the PDF through ACEC or APWA.
Primary DOJ documents for United States v. AIA (1972 and 1990) returned 401/403; the antitrust finding rests on trade press, and decree language could not be quoted verbatim.

The Federal Register text of the June 27, 2024 DFARS final rule (89 FR 53502, Case 2024-D019) remains unfetched (bot-blocked); the statute and current DFARS text were fetched directly, so only the rule's publication metadata rests on federalregister.gov search-result metadata.

Applicability limits on every fee curve found: all are public building or civil schedules whose smallest tabulated size ($100K Delaware, $1M Washington) sits at or above GMZ's typical project, each reverts to 'negotiated' below its floor, and each covers full basic services including bidding and construction administration (31 percent of the fee in Washington's split). The curves bound GMZ's bracket only by direction (percentages rise as size falls) plus the stated phase-split adjustment; no source publishes a design-only percentage curve.

No peer-reviewed study of design cost share for landscape or site-work projects specifically was found; the inverse-size and PE-ratio evidence comes from highway and bridge research (NC, VA), which transfers as a structural pattern, not as numbers.

Fee-angle audit correction log: (1) Delaware's claimed 2-4 point renovation premium 'in every bracket' was false (narrows to 1-2.5 points at $10M-$15M) and was corrected; mid-bracket values rest on a single extraction pass and the page is undated. (2) The WA remodel 'three percentage points' was restated as the source's literal 'up to three percent' with the points reading flagged as interpretation. (3) The AIA antitrust causal claim about ASLA was softened to consistency. (4) The DFARS finding was upgraded to high confidence on direct statute verification. All other figures and quotes survived verification unchanged.

The Caltrans PE anchor is from the FY 2012-13 annual report; more recent project delivery reports were not audited, so whether the three-year PE average and the 20 percent target structure remain similar today is unverified. Cite it as a historical statutory-target anchor, not a current statistic.

Escalator-angle audit result (2026-08-15): all 14 findings survived verification; every source URL was fetched, every figure traced, every quote checked verbatim. Corrections were refinements: the SF bimonthly-schedule caveat was tightened (the even-month pattern comes from series data, not the release text), the gardening CPI finding now cites the directly verifiable timeseries page, the material-change quote was extended to the full statutory phrase, and the Fairfield and Los Gatos findings gained contractor/district identification and the $878,860 five-year base figure.

OEWS year-over-year wage movement could not be computed from primary sources: the BLS API serves only the May 2025 vintage (requests for 2024 and 2026 return 'No Data Available'), archive routes failed, and third-party pages quoting May 2024 figures were rejected under source discipline.

The exact current metro title for OEWS area 41860 could not be confirmed from a fetched BLS page; findings reference the area code. The CPI metro (San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward, covering Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, San Francisco and San Mateo counties) is a distinct delineation from the OEWS metro and neither includes Santa Clara County.

The gardening and lawncare series (CUUR0000SEHP02) returns only scattered 2025 months (May, July, September; October footnoted unavailable), so the +12.3% July-over-July print cannot be cross-checked against a continuous monthly run; the arithmetic is exact on retrieved values but treat the level with care.

The San Francisco-area CPI-W series (the index family the Fairfield precedent and the Labor Code formula use) was not pulled; only SF CPI-U was retrieved. Fetch the SF CPI-W series and its latest 12-month change before drafting a CPI-W-pegged clause.

No executed grounds-maintenance escalation clause from a San Mateo County city was captured; the nearest verified precedents are Los Gatos (Santa Clara County) and Fairfield (Solano County). Elk Grove's 2026 landscape maintenance RFP and an LA County parks COLA cap were identified in search but not fetched, so they are not cited as findings.

B&P 17602 quotes were verified across three independent leginfo fetches and all matched verbatim; however, subdivision lettering has not been independently verified against a raw page render, so findings quote text without asserting subdivision letters.

Local city minimum wage ordinances on the Peninsula (e.g. Redwood City, Menlo Park and Palo Alto set rates above the state floor with their own CPI formulas) were not pulled; the state $17.40 figure understates the binding wage floor in several GMZ service-area cities. The DIR FAQ itself carves out employers covered by a higher local minimum.

No peer-reviewed evidence supports the specific 30-day or six-month follow-up timing. The two-touch cadence is practitioner convention; the literature supports post-purchase gratitude contact and the value of retention generally, but no study tests contact timing for home services.

Carey et al. (1976): neither the effect magnitude (the circulated ~70% purchase increase) nor the design details (jewelry store, three telephone-call conditions) are verifiable from any fetchable source; Sage and EBSCO are paywalled. Only the citation and Grant & Gino's qualitative characterization are verified, and the design details were stripped from the claim on audit.

No peer-reviewed effect sizes exist for referral, follow-up, or review economics in landscaping or home services specifically. Every surviving study is banking, a social-network platform, restaurants, or e-commerce; direction transfers to GMZ, magnitude does not.

Kumar, Petersen & Leone (2010): the often-quoted 10-30% profit increase from targeted referral campaigns appears only in secondary summaries; the fetched peer-reviewed abstract contains no such figure and the full text is paywalled. Treat any such magnitude as unverified.
de Matos et al. (2007) meta-analysis: the number of pooled studies and effect sizes is not disclosed in the fetched abstract; full text paywalled, so magnitudes are unverified.

Reichheld & Sasser (1990) original industry-by-industry defection figures could not be fetched; only Bain's 2001 one-line summary was verifiable, and it is consultancy-tier evidence with undisclosed method.

No published CLV framework compares a recurring maintenance account to a one-time design/build client within contracting; Gupta, Lehmann & Stuart (2004) is the nearest general framework and its retention > margin > acquisition elasticity ordering is the usable takeaway.

No peer-reviewed study links post-completion follow-up contact directly to online review rates for local service firms; Burtch et al. (2018) covers solicitation mechanics but in Chinese e-commerce, and platform policies (Yelp and Google prohibit incentivized reviews) limit which treatment arms are usable.

Review-platform effects for contractors specifically (Houzz, Google Business Profile) have no peer-reviewed causal literature comparable to the Yelp restaurant studies; the vendor surveys that exist were rejected under source discipline.

Version caveat affecting four findings: the fetched files for Trusov et al., Luca, Gupta et al., and Anderson & Magruder are pre-publication or author-hosted versions rather than typeset journal articles. Figures were verified against the fetched versions; typeset versions may differ in minor details.

findings.claim: B&P 7027.5(a) grants a C-27 licensee design authority only for work 'to be performed and supervised by that contractor', so the statutory text ties the design right to the contractor's own anticipated construction rather than to design as a freestanding service.
findings.quote: (a) A landscape contractor working within the classification for which the license is issued may design systems or facilities for work to be performed and supervised by that contractor.
findings.sourceName: California Business and Professions Code § 7027.5, leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (official)
findings.publishedDate: Last amended Stats. 2012, Ch. 537, Sec. 1 (AB 1750), effective 2013-01-01; verified current 2026-08-15
findings.bearsOn: GMZ's paid design-only agreement: whether a design phase sold under its own contract, where the client might not proceed to construction or might take the plans elsewhere, sits inside the C-27 design authority. Counsel must construe 'to be performed and supervised by that contractor'.
findings.caveat: The statute nowhere addresses what happens if the designed work is never built or is built by someone else; no case, AG opinion, or CSLB guidance resolving that was found. Subdivision (e) further limits the grant, verbatim per leginfo (verified 2026-08-15): 'Nothing in this section authorizes a landscape contractor to engage in or perform activities that require a license pursuant to the Professional Engineers Act (Chapter 7 (commencing with Section 6700)).'

findings.claim: B&P 5641.4 exempts a licensed landscape contractor from the Landscape Architects Practice Act for design of work the contractor will perform and supervise, but forbids use of the title 'landscape architect'.
findings.quote: A landscape contractor licensed under the statutes of this state, insofar as they work within the classification for which the license is issued, may design systems and facilities for work to be performed and supervised by that landscape contractor and is exempt from this chapter, except that a landscape contractor shall not use the title "landscape architect" unless they hold a license as required under this chapter.
findings.sourceName: California Business and Professions Code § 5641.4, leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (official)
findings.publishedDate: Last amended Stats. 2024, Ch. 482, Sec. 25 (SB 1452), effective 2025-01-01; verified current 2026-08-15
findings.bearsOn: The same 'performed and supervised by that contractor' limit appears in both the Contractors' State License Law (7027.5) and the LA Practice Act (5641.4); counsel can read them in pari materia. Also a hard rule for GMZ marketing and the design agreement: never the words 'landscape architect' or 'landscape architectural'.
findings.caveat: Recently amended (effective 2025); any older secondary summaries citing pre-SB 1452 wording are out of date.

findings.claim: The C-27 classification definition in 16 CCR 832.27 describes only construction-side activity (constructs, maintains, repairs, installs, subcontracts, prepares and grades land) and assigns no design activity to the contractor; the only occurrence of 'design' is the participle 'designed' describing the improved areas, so a C-27's design authority rests entirely on B&P 7027.5 and 5641.4, not on the regulation.
findings.quote: A landscape contractor constructs, maintains, repairs, installs, or subcontracts the development of landscape systems and facilities for public and private gardens and other areas which are designed to aesthetically, architecturally, horticulturally, or functionally improve the grounds within or surrounding a structure or a tract or plot of land. In connection therewith, a landscape contractor prepares and grades plots and areas of land for the installation of any architectural, horticultural and decorative treatment or arrangement.
findings.sourceName: 16 CCR § 832.27 as reproduced on CSLB's C-27 classification page (regulator publication)
findings.publishedDate: Regulation amendment filed 1988-06-01, operative 1988-07-01 (Register 88, No. 23) per Cornell LII reproduction; CSLB page itself undated, fetched 2026-08-15
findings.bearsOn: Scope description for GMZ's license classification; confirms maintenance ('maintains, repairs') is squarely in-classification for the recurring accounts line, and that the design agreement must lean on the statutes, not the regulation.
findings.caveat: Verified on CSLB's classification page 2026-08-15, which shows 'Authority cited: Sections 7008 and 7059, Reference: Sections 7058 and 7059 (Business and Professions Code)'. The canonical govt.westlaw CCR portal was not fetched; the Register history rests on the Cornell LII reproduction. Original claim wording ('the word design does not appear') was corrected in audit: 'designed' does appear, but only describing the areas, not as a contractor activity.

findings.claim: B&P 5615 defines the practice of landscape architecture to include planning, design, preparation of drawings, construction documents and specifications, and responsible construction observation for landscape preservation, development and enhancement, which is the field the 5641.4 contractor exemption carves GMZ out of.
findings.quote: A person who practices landscape architecture within the meaning and intent of this article is a person who offers or performs professional services, for the purpose of landscape preservation, development and enhancement, such as consultation, investigation, reconnaissance, research, planning, design, preparation of drawings, construction documents and specifications, and responsible construction observation.
findings.sourceName: California Business and Professions Code § 5615, leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (official)
findings.publishedDate: Last amended Stats. 2006, Ch. 564, Sec. 9, effective 2007-01-01; verified current 2026-08-15
findings.bearsOn: Baseline definition counsel needs to measure GMZ's design deliverables against: everything GMZ's paid design step produces is inside this definition unless the 5641.4 exemption covers it.
findings.caveat: The core definitional sentence is verified verbatim; the section's further enumerated activities (site planning, irrigation design, collaboration on infrastructure, field observation, and the prohibition on practicing architecture or engineering) were confirmed present but returned summarized, not quoted.

findings.claim: Unlicensed practice of landscape architecture, or use of the title or any words implying licensure, is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of $100 to $5,000 and/or up to six months in county jail under B&P 5640.
findings.quote: It is a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of not less than one hundred dollars ($100) nor more than five thousand dollars ($5,000) or by imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding six months, or by both that fine and imprisonment, for a person to do any of the following without possessing a valid, unrevoked license as provided in this chapter: (a) Engage in the practice of landscape architecture. (b) Use the title or term "landscape architect," "landscape architecture," "landscape architectural," or any other titles, words, or abbreviations that would imply or indicate that they are a landscape architect, as defined in Section 5615.
findings.sourceName: California Business and Professions Code § 5640, leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (official)
findings.publishedDate: Last amended Stats. 2024, Ch. 482, Sec. 23 (SB 1452), effective 2025-01-01; verified current 2026-08-15
findings.figure: $100-$5,000 fine; up to 6 months county jail
findings.bearsOn: The penalty exposure that makes the wording of GMZ's website, design agreement and proposals matter: 'landscape design by our licensed landscape contractor' is safe; 'landscape architectural services' is a misdemeanor.
findings.caveat: Subdivisions (c) (use of a licensed LA's stamp) and (d) (advertising or displaying signs suggesting licensure) extend the prohibition; audit confirmed the four-subdivision structure and penalty amounts, with the (a)/(b) text verified near-verbatim.

findings.claim: B&P 5641 lets any unlicensed person prepare conceptual design drawings and plant-selection plans for a single family dwelling, but requires that construction documents, details, specifications, and grading and drainage plans be prepared by 'a licensed professional as required by law'.
findings.quote: This chapter shall not be deemed to prohibit any person from preparing drawings for the conceptual design and placement of tangible objects and landscape features or plans, drawings, and specifications for the selection, placement, or use of plants for a single family dwelling. Construction documents, details, or specifications for the tangible objects or landscape features, and alteration of site requiring grading and drainage plans shall be prepared by a licensed professional as required by law.
findings.sourceName: California Business and Professions Code § 5641, leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (official)
findings.publishedDate: Last amended Stats. 2004, Ch. 691, Sec. 12, effective 2005-01-01; verified current 2026-08-15
findings.bearsOn: Draws the line between what unlicensed 'garden designers' on the Peninsula may sell (conceptual only, single family dwellings) and what GMZ's C-27 license adds (construction-level documents for its own work); useful both for the design agreement's deliverables list and for positioning against unlicensed competitors.
findings.caveat: 'A licensed professional as required by law' is not defined in the section; the LATC's Permitted Practices document reads the licensed-professional universe to include C-27 contractors via 5641.4 (see latc-permitted-practices-c27-construction-documents). The LATC document also confirms the parallel exemptions for property owners (5641.1), nurserypersons (5641.2), architects/engineers (5641.3), golf course architects (5641.5) and irrigation consultants (5641.6).

findings.claim: The LATC's 'Permitted Practices in California' reference states that a C-27 licensee 'may design systems and facilities for work to be performed and supervised by that contractor which may include landscape construction documents and landscape drawings with specifications and details', while unlicensed persons 'may NOT prepare construction documents, details, or specifications for tangible landscape objects or landscape features' and 'may NOT prepare grading and drainage plans for the alteration of sites'.
findings.quote: LANDSCAPE CONTRACTORS. Hold a C-27 (landscaping contractor) license. May design systems and facilities for work to be performed and supervised by that contractor which may include landscape construction documents and landscape drawings with specifications and details. Are exempt from the Landscape Architects Practice Act insofar as they are providing services in which they are licensed to do so. APPLICABLE REGULATION/STATUTES: Section 832.27 of the California Code of Regulations, Title 16, Division 8 and Section 5641.4 and 7027.5 of the BPC. ... [UNLICENSED PERSONS] May NOT prepare construction documents, details, or specifications for tangible landscape objects or landscape features. May NOT prepare grading and drainage plans for the alteration of sites.
findings.sourceName: Landscape Architects Technical Committee, 'Permitted Practices in California' (regulator publication, PDF)
findings.publishedDate: September 2023 per the PDF's XMP metadata; undated on its face
findings.bearsOn: The clearest regulator statement found that a C-27's design deliverables may go all the way to construction documents with specifications and details, i.e. GMZ's paid design package can be construction-ready, provided the tie to GMZ-performed work holds.
findings.caveat: Full PDF text extracted and quote verified verbatim in audit 2026-08-15. The document disclaims legal effect: 'While every effort has been made to ensure the accuracy of this document, it does not have legal effect. Should any difference or error occur, the law will take precedence.' It is guidance, not regulation, and it does not address design-only engagements where construction never follows. An earlier note that LATC's FAQ page repeats the rule was removed in audit because that page was never fetched.

findings.claim: B&P 7151.2 defines 'home improvement contract' as an agreement between a contractor and an owner or tenant 'for the performance of a home improvement ... and includes all labor, services, and materials to be furnished and performed thereunder', without expressly including or excluding a design-only agreement.
findings.quote: "Home improvement contract" means an agreement, whether oral or written, or contained in one or more documents, between a contractor and an owner or between a contractor and a tenant, regardless of the number of residence or dwelling units contained in the building in which the tenant resides, if the work is to be performed in, to, or upon the residence or dwelling unit of the tenant, for the performance of a home improvement as defined in Section 7151, and includes all labor, services, and materials to be furnished and performed thereunder.
findings.sourceName: California Business and Professions Code § 7151.2, leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (official)
findings.publishedDate: Last amended Stats. 1991, Ch. 1160, Sec. 42; verified current 2026-08-15
findings.bearsOn: Whether GMZ's standalone paid design agreement must carry the full 7159 home-improvement-contract apparatus (statutory notices, cancellation rights, 7159.5 deposit cap). The text is silent on design-only; the answer turns on the definitional chain into 7151 and Civil Code 1689.5.
findings.caveat: The section's second sentence extends the definition to salesperson agreements 'for the sale, installation, or furnishing of home improvement goods or services', which pulls in the 7151/1689.5 chain quoted in the next finding. No statute, regulation, or published guidance expressly classifying a contractor's design-only agreement was found.

findings.claim: B&P 7151 makes 'the furnishing of home improvement services' itself a 'home improvement', and defines those services through Civil Code 1689.5 as services 'bought in connection with the improvement of real property', a chain broad enough that counsel could place a paid design agreement inside the home-improvement-contract regime.
findings.quote: "Home improvement" shall also mean the installation of home improvement goods or the furnishing of home improvement services. For purposes of this chapter, "home improvement goods or services" means goods and services, as defined in Section 1689.5 of the Civil Code, which are bought in connection with the improvement of real property. [CIV 1689.5(d):] "Services" means work, labor and services, including, but not limited to, services furnished in connection with the repair, restoration, alteration, or improvement of residential premises, or services furnished in connection with the sale or repair of goods
findings.sourceName: California Business and Professions Code § 7151 and Civil Code § 1689.5, leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (official)
findings.publishedDate: BPC 7151 last amended Stats. 2021, Ch. 249, Sec. 1 (SB 757), effective 2022-01-01; CIV 1689.5 last amended Stats. 2020, Ch. 158, Sec. 4 (AB 2471), effective 2021-01-01; both verified current 2026-08-15
findings.bearsOn: The safest-practice conclusion for GMZ: because 'services bought in connection with the improvement of real property' plausibly reaches a design fee, drafting the design agreement to comply with 7159 (and honoring the three-day cancel right) costs little and forecloses the argument. Counsel should confirm.
findings.caveat: 7151 also lists 'landscaping' and 'fences' expressly among home improvements (verified). CIV 1689.5(d)'s exclusions cover attorneys, real estate professionals, securities dealers, physicians, optometrists and dentists, not design professionals. CIV 1689.5(a) sets the home solicitation threshold at $25 or more 'made at other than appropriate trade premises'; 1689.5(f) defines senior citizen as 'an individual who is 65 years of age or older'. The Civil Code section was fetched at https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1689.5. The 'could place a design agreement inside the regime' step is the researcher's inference, not stated in any source, hence medium confidence.

findings.claim: Under B&P 7159(e)(6), the Three-Day (or Five-Day, for seniors) Right to Cancel notice must be included in every home improvement contract unless the contract was negotiated at the contractor's place of business, is subject to the Seven-Day Right to Cancel, or is an alarm company contract; the notice's operative text starts the clock when the buyer receives a signed and dated copy of the contract containing the notice.
findings.quote: (A) The notice ... entitled "Three-Day Right to Cancel," or entitled "Five-Day Right to Cancel" for contracts with a senior citizen, shall be provided to the buyer unless the contract is: (i) Negotiated at the contractor's place of business. (ii) Subject to the "Seven-Day Right to Cancel," as set forth in paragraph (7). (iii) Subject to licensure under the Alarm Company Act... [B](i): "You, the buyer, have the right to cancel this contract within three business days. You may cancel by emailing, mailing, faxing, or delivering a written notice to the contractor at the contractor's place of business by midnight of the third business day after you received a signed and dated copy of the contract that includes this notice." (ii): References to "three" and "third" ... shall be changed to "five" and "fifth," respectively, for a buyer who is a senior citizen.
findings.sourceName: California Business and Professions Code § 7159(e)(6), leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (official)
findings.publishedDate: Last amended Stats. 2025, Ch. 585, Sec. 1.5 (SB 517), effective 2026-01-01; quoted provisions verified present in the current text 2026-08-15
findings.figure: 3 business days; 5 for buyers 65 or older
findings.bearsOn: GMZ signs design and construction agreements at clients' homes on the Peninsula, so the notice is required in both; because clients skew 65+, in Atherton, Hillsborough and Woodside especially, the Five-Day variant will often be the correct one, and the cancellation clock runs from delivery of the signed copy containing the notice.
findings.caveat: Audit correction: 7159 was amended by SB 517 effective 2026-01-01, which the original research missed (it recorded the date as unknown); the (e)(6)(A) trigger, (B)(i) notice text, (B)(ii) senior substitution, and (a)(2) service-and-repair carve-out were all re-verified in the current post-SB 517 text, but what else SB 517 changed in the section was not diffed. 7159 is long and was quoted by targeted extracts, not reproduced end to end; counsel should pull the full current section, including paragraph (7)'s Seven-Day Right to Cancel. 7159(a)(2), verified verbatim: the section 'does not apply to service and repair contracts that are subject to Section 7159.10, if the contract for the applicable services complies with Sections 7159.10 to 7159.14, inclusive.'

findings.claim: CSLB's consumer guidance frames the three-day right as arising 'unless the contract is negotiated at the contractor's place of business, and/or the contract price is under $25', importing the $25 threshold from Civil Code 1689.5's home solicitation definition even though B&P 7159(e)(6)(A) itself contains no dollar threshold.
findings.quote: Unless the contract is negotiated at the contractor's place of business, and/or the contract price is under $25, the buyer qualifies for a three-day right to cancel. ... Starting in 2021, seniors (those 65 and older) will have five days to cancel the following transactions: home solicitation contracts, home improvement contracts, Property Assessed Clean Energy assessment contracts, service and repair contracts, and seminar sales contracts (AB 2471).
findings.sourceName: CSLB, 'Home Improvement Contracts — Warnings and Exceptions' (regulator publication)
findings.publishedDate: unknown (page undated, confirmed in audit 2026-08-15; references AB 2471, so post-2020)
findings.figure: $25 threshold (from CIV 1689.5(a), not from 7159)
findings.bearsOn: The reconciliation counsel was asked for: the statutory trigger in 7159(e)(6)(A) is purely locational (negotiated at the contractor's place of business or not), while CSLB's framing blends in the Home Solicitation Sales Act's $25 floor; both sources are now quoted so the design agreement's notice block can be drafted to satisfy the stricter reading.
findings.caveat: Consumer-facing guidance, not law; where it diverges from 7159's text, the statute controls. The page also states, verbatim: 'The right to a three-day notice automatically is canceled the moment the contract is signed and the contractor begins working on a "Service and Repair" contract.' DCA Legal Guide K-10 (dca.ca.gov/publications/legal_guides/k_10.pdf) surfaced in search as a further T1 reconciliation source but was not fetched. Guidance page not yet updated against the SB 517 (2026) amendment of 7159, so treat its framing as potentially stale.

findings.claim: A 'service and repair contract' escaping full 7159 formalities must satisfy all four of B&P 7159.10(a)(1)'s conditions: price $750 or less, buyer-initiated contact, no selling beyond what the particular problem reasonably requires, and no payment due or accepted until the work is completed.
findings.quote: (A) The contract amount is seven hundred fifty dollars ($750) or less. (B) The prospective buyer initiated contact with the contractor to request the work. (C) The contractor does not sell the buyer goods or services beyond those reasonably necessary to take care of the particular problem that caused the buyer to contact the contractor. (D) No payment is due, or accepted by the contractor, until the work is completed.
findings.sourceName: California Business and Professions Code § 7159.10, leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (official)
findings.publishedDate: Last amended Stats. 2020, Ch. 158, Sec. 3 (AB 2471), effective 2021-01-01; verified current 2026-08-15
findings.figure: $750 or less; payment only on completion
findings.bearsOn: New for the maintenance line beyond Study 001: small ad-hoc repairs on GMZ's recurring accounts can use the service-and-repair form only if the client called first, GMZ does not upsell beyond the presenting problem, and GMZ collects nothing until done; CSLB's guidance page adds that the three-day notice right is canceled the moment the contract is signed and work begins on a service and repair contract.
findings.caveat: Condition (D) means the service-and-repair route is incompatible with any advance payment. Work exceeding $750 or contractor-solicited work falls back into full 7159 territory.

findings.claim: B&P 7027.1 makes it a misdemeanor, with a fine of $700 to $1,000, to advertise for construction or work of improvement without holding a valid license in the classification so advertised, and defines advertising to include electronic transmission.
findings.quote: (a) It is a misdemeanor for any person to advertise for construction or work of improvement covered by this chapter unless that person holds a valid license under this chapter in the classification so advertised... (c) A violation of this section is punishable by a fine of not less than seven hundred dollars ($700) and not more than one thousand dollars ($1,000)...
findings.sourceName: California Business and Professions Code § 7027.1, leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (official)
findings.publishedDate: Last amended Stats. 1998, Ch. 599, Sec. 2, effective 1999-01-01; verified current 2026-08-15
findings.bearsOn: The GMZ website is 'electronic transmission' advertising: everything it offers (design, build, maintenance, fencing, irrigation) must sit within the C-27 classification or be framed as subcontracted; closes Study 001's open item on 7027.1.
findings.caveat: Subdivision (b)'s advertising definition was verified to include 'any card, sign, or device', newspaper/magazine placement, and 'airwave or any electronic transmission', but the audit fetch returned (b) partially paraphrased, so the original finding's longer (b) quote was trimmed to the phrases verified verbatim. The section targets unlicensed or misclassified advertising; a valid C-27 advertising in-classification work is compliant. Subdivision (d) lets the registrar cite via 7028.7 or 7099.10.

findings.claim: B&P 7027.3 punishes willful, intent-to-defraud use of a contractor's license number that does not correspond to one's own currently valid license with a fine up to $10,000 and/or up to one year's imprisonment, and applies to licensed and unlicensed persons alike.
findings.quote: Any person, licensed or unlicensed, who willfully and intentionally uses, with intent to defraud, a contractor's license number that does not correspond to the number on a currently valid contractor's license held by that person, is punishable by a fine not exceeding ten thousand dollars ($10,000), or by imprisonment in state prison, or in county jail for not more than one year, or by both that fine and imprisonment.
findings.sourceName: California Business and Professions Code § 7027.3, leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (official)
findings.publishedDate: Last amended Stats. 2001, Ch. 728, Sec. 54, effective 2002-01-01 (audit corrected from the original's 2002-01-02)
findings.figure: Up to $10,000 fine; up to 1 year imprisonment
findings.bearsOn: Closes Study 001's second open item: 7027.3 is a fraud statute about misusing a license number, not about classification scope; for GMZ it simply reinforces keeping the CSLB number accurate everywhere it appears (which the site's one-fact-one-home rule already enforces).
findings.caveat: Requires willfulness and intent to defraud; an innocent typo in a license number is not within the section's terms, though it invites other problems. Penalties are cumulative with other state law, and the registrar may cite unlicensed violators.

findings.claim: BAWSCA's Lawn Be Gone! turf-replacement rebate page lists agency-set rates in GMZ's San Mateo County towns: $2.00/sq ft in Redwood City, $3.00/sq ft in Menlo Park, $4.00/sq ft in Mid-Peninsula Water District, and $1.00/sq ft in Hillsborough, plus a $300 flat rain-garden rebate where participating, and the client must receive a Notice to Proceed from the water provider before any lawn is removed; Palo Alto is not on the participating-agency list.
findings.quote: To receive the rebate, you must submit an application and receive a Notice to Proceed from your water provider before removing your lawn.
findings.sourceName: BAWSCA Water Conservation Program, Lawn Be Gone! (bayareaconservation.org)
findings.publishedDate: unknown (page undated; linked documents reference FY19-20 and FY 20-21)
findings.geography: BAWSCA member agencies, San Mateo County, CA
findings.figure: $1.00-$4.00 per sq ft by agency; +$300 rain garden
findings.bearsOn: The 'your water supplier pays you to replace your lawn' sales claim: GMZ can cite a town-specific rate in proposals, but must sequence jobs so the client holds a Notice to Proceed before demo day, or the rebate is forfeited.
findings.caveat: Rates and quote verified on the fetched page 2026-08-15, but the page is undated and its linked documents reference FY19-20/FY 20-21, so the displayed rates may lag the current fiscal year; confirm the current-year rate with the specific agency before quoting a dollar figure to a client. Per-agency maximum caps are not stated on the page. That Mid-Peninsula WD covers Belmont and part of San Carlos, and that artificial turf is ineligible, were not verified on this page. The researcher's earlier 'FY 2026-27' reference could not be reproduced.

findings.claim: Valley Water's Landscape Rebate Program for Santa Clara County pays $2/sq ft for lawn conversion with a $3,000 default cap for single-family residential (a $6,000 cost-share cap in some areas), requires a completed pre-inspection and a written Notice to Proceed before any lawn removal or material purchase, and states current funding lasts until June 30, 2027 or until depleted.
findings.quote: Do not begin removal of your lawn/pool or the purchase of materials for your project until you have received a written Notice to Proceed from Valley Water.
findings.sourceName: Santa Clara Valley Water District, Landscape Rebates
findings.publishedDate: unknown (page undated; states funding through June 30, 2027; fetched 2026-08-15)
findings.geography: Santa Clara County, CA (includes Los Altos and Palo Alto addresses)
findings.figure: $2/sq ft base; $3,000 SFR default cap ($6,000 cost-share cap in some areas); funding through 2027-06-30 or until depleted
findings.bearsOn: Rebate line in Los Altos and Palo Alto proposals and the job-sequencing rule GMZ must follow: the lawn must still be in place at pre-inspection, so design-phase scheduling has to leave the turf untouched until the NTP arrives.
findings.caveat: Projects started before the written NTP are permanently ineligible. A 75 sq ft minimum conversion area reported in a Valley Water support article does not appear on the main program page and remains unconfirmed.

findings.claim: Cal Water's lawn-to-garden turf rebate requires pre-approval before the project begins, requires at least 3 approved plants per 100 sq ft converted, excludes artificial turf, and does not publish its per-square-foot rate on the public conservation page; the rate is only accessible through its customer Conservation Portal.
findings.quote: Pre-approval is required prior to beginning your project. ... 3 approved plants per 100 square foot converted is required. ... Artificial turf does not qualify for this rebate.
findings.sourceName: California Water Service, Rebates and Conservation Programs
findings.publishedDate: unknown (page undated; fetched 2026-08-15)
findings.geography: Cal Water service areas overlapping GMZ territory
findings.figure: 3 approved plants per 100 sq ft; $/sq ft rate not published on public page
findings.bearsOn: GMZ cannot quote a rebate dollar figure to Cal Water-served clients from public pages; the honest sales move is to have the client open a Conservation Portal account during the design phase.
findings.caveat: The missing rate is the finding: no per-sq-ft figure is publicly published. Which specific GMZ towns fall in Cal Water's Bear Gulch and Mid-Peninsula districts was not verified from a primary source.

findings.claim: Menlo Park enforces its own water-efficient landscaping ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 12.44), applying to all new landscapes exceeding 500 sq ft and rehabilitated landscapes exceeding 1,000 sq ft associated with projects requiring city review and approval, with a landscape plan showing planting by species, hydrozone and WUCOLS classification, an irrigation plan, and post-construction Certificate of Completion and Landscape Audit Report completed by a licensed auditor or the designer.
findings.quote: These reports must be completed by a licensed auditor or the designer. ... Proposed planting by species, hydro-zone and Water Use Classification of Landscape Species (WUCOLS).
findings.sourceName: City of Menlo Park, Water-efficient landscaping ordinance (Public Works Engineering Division)
findings.publishedDate: unknown (city page undated; underlying Ordinance 1015 adoption date not confirmed from a primary source)
findings.figure: 500 sq ft (new) / 1,000 sq ft (rehabilitated) thresholds; Prescriptive A requires 75% of proposed planting at low water use (average WUCOLS 0.3)
findings.bearsOn: Scope and price of GMZ's paid design step in Menlo Park: the audit-report and WUCOLS documentation duties belong in the design agreement, and the 1,000 sq ft rehabilitated threshold differs from the impression that 500 sq ft always triggers documentation.
findings.caveat: The city page summarizes Chapter 12.44; the codified chapter text (eCode360) is bot-blocked and was not read verbatim. Applicability is limited to projects requiring city review and approval, so a landscape-only job needing no city permit may fall outside it; confirm with the city for permit-free scopes.

findings.claim: In Atherton, a tree 48 inches or more in circumference (measured 48 inches above grade) outside the Building or Dwelling Area is permit-protected; inside the Building or Dwelling Area only native oaks (Quercus) of 48 inches or more remain protected, and four listed species (three acacias and Ailanthus altissima) are never heritage trees. A non-dead/dangerous removal requires Planning Commission approval with a non-refundable $750 application fee, a tree survey and arborist report, filing 19 days before the hearing, and, at the Commission's discretion, replacement planting per removed tree of three 15-gallon trees, or two 24-inch box trees, or one 15-gallon plus one 36-inch box tree.
findings.quote: The tree, located anywhere on the lot, smaller than 48" in circumference, when measured 48" above grade [may be removed without a permit] ... All other trees cannot be removed unless a permit has been issued to the property owner or tree professional. ... Non-refundable $750.00 application fee.
findings.sourceName: Town of Atherton, Tree Removal Procedure (official town handout, DocumentCenter)
findings.publishedDate: unknown (undated town handout implementing AMC Chapter 8.10)
findings.figure: 48 in. circumference at 48 in. above grade; $750 fee; 19-day filing lead; discretionary replacement up to 3 trees per tree removed; $2,000 minimum deposit if environmental assessment required; permit void if unused within one year
findings.bearsOn: Schedule and contingency on Atherton design/build jobs: one protected tree in the layout adds a month-plus Planning Commission cycle (fourth Wednesday monthly), $750+, and an arborist retainer; the design agreement should surface this before construction pricing.
findings.caveat: The handout is undated, so the $750 fee and procedure details may have changed. Measurement-height conflict: this handout says 48 inches above grade while secondary summaries of current AMC 8.10.020 say 54 inches; the code host was Cloudflare-blocked, so confirm with Atherton Planning. Dead or dangerous trees follow a separate Town Arborist/Building Official permit path.

findings.claim: Menlo Park defines a heritage tree as any California-native oak (Quercus) with trunk circumference of 31.4 inches (10 in. diameter) or more, or any other tree at 47.1 inches circumference (15 in. diameter) or more, measured 54 inches above natural grade, and requires a city permit before removal or before pruning exceeding 25 percent of the canopy, with required arborist reports prepared by a consulting arborist from the city's approved list.
findings.quote: All trees other than oaks which have a trunk with a circumference of 47.1 inches (diameter of fifteen (15) inches) or more, measured fifty-four (54) inches above natural grade. ... An oak tree (Quercus) which is native to California and has a trunk with a circumference of 31.4 inches (diameter of ten (10) inches) or more, measured at fifty-four (54) inches above natural grade.
findings.sourceName: City of Menlo Park, city news 'Preserve or remove? The Heritage Tree Ordinance' (quoting Municipal Code Ch. 13.24)
findings.figure: Oaks: 31.4 in. circumference (10 in. dia.); other trees: 47.1 in. (15 in. dia.); measured at 54 in. above natural grade; permit at >25% canopy pruning
findings.bearsOn: Menlo Park job scoping: a 10-inch oak is a small tree, so ordinary planting-bed redesigns can trip the ordinance; GMZ must budget for an arborist from the city's approved list, not its own preferred one.
findings.caveat: Definition quoted from the city's own 2023 article summarizing Ch. 13.24; the codified chapter (eCode360) was bot-blocked and not read verbatim. A root-pruning threshold (the researcher's original 'or roots' clause) was not confirmed by the cited article; check Ch. 13.24 before relying on a root-work trigger.

findings.claim: Per Canopy's summary of Palo Alto's Tree Protection Ordinance as updated in June 2022 (the first substantive change since 2002), coast live oak, valley oak, blue oak, California black oak, bigleaf maple and California incense cedar are protected at 11.5 in. trunk diameter, coast redwood at 18 in., and all other non-invasive, non-high-water-use species at 15 in.
findings.sourceName: Canopy (Palo Alto urban-forestry nonprofit), Palo Alto Tree Protection Ordinance summary
findings.publishedDate: unknown (describes ordinance update of June 2022; page undated)
findings.figure: 11.5 in. dia. (listed natives), 18 in. (redwood), 15 in. (all other species)
findings.bearsOn: Palo Alto design/build scoping: at a 15-inch all-species threshold, most established residential lots contain protected trees, so tree disclosure belongs in GMZ's Palo Alto design intake checklist.
findings.caveat: No T1 was fetchable: paloalto.gov PDFs and the amlegal-hosted PAMC returned 403s in this audit, matching the researcher's report. Materially, search results indicate a 2024 amendment (Ordinance 5612) following a 2023 council effort to pare the rules back, and its effect on these thresholds is unverified; the Canopy page may be stale. The original 'roughly tripled the number of protected trees' clause was removed because it does not appear on the cited source. Verify against current PAMC 8.10 before putting any threshold in client-facing material.

findings.claim: In unincorporated San Mateo County, grading qualifies for a permit exemption only when it meets the criteria of Section 8603 of the county Grading Regulations, including that total cut and fill amounts total 250 cubic yards or less; exemptions are processed either over-the-counter at no fee or as a formal exemption with a fee of roughly $720 to $1,700 and 2-4 weeks processing.
findings.quote: grading operations that would involve cut and fill amounts that total 250 cubic yards or less
findings.sourceName: County of San Mateo Planning and Building, Grading Permit Exemption
findings.publishedDate: unknown (page undated; fetched 2026-08-15)
findings.geography: Unincorporated San Mateo County, CA (includes pockets such as Emerald Hills, North Fair Oaks and West Menlo Park)
findings.figure: 250 cubic yards total cut+fill exemption ceiling; formal exemption fee ~$720-$1,700; 2-4 weeks
findings.bearsOn: Whether a hillside cut-and-fill job on an unincorporated parcel carries a county permit line item; GMZ intake should confirm incorporation status of the address, since a Redwood City mailing address can be an unincorporated parcel.
findings.caveat: The page says Section 8603 criteria go beyond the 250 cy ceiling ('including, but not limited to') without enumerating them; the unincorporated-pocket list is background knowledge, not verified on this page. Reported staff-vs-hearing review tiers above 1,000 cy were not verified and are excluded.

findings.claim: Portola Valley reviews Site Development Permit grading in tiers: under 100 cubic yards reviewed generally by the Town Engineer, Town Geologist and Town Planner; 100 to 1,000 cubic yards, or cuts/fills exceeding 5 feet, reviewed by those staff plus other site development committee members and the ASCC; over 1,000 cubic yards (or vegetation removal) adds the Planning Commission. Fences 6 ft or under need no building permit, but any fence regardless of height within building setbacks, on a property line or adjacent to a trail easement needs a town fence permit, and the town counts compacted gravel and rock areas as impervious surface.
findings.quote: A building permit is not required to build any fence 6' or less in height. However, when a fence, regardless of height, is to be built within your property's building setbacks, on your property line, or adjacent to a trail easement, a fence permit is required.
findings.sourceName: Town of Portola Valley, Planning FAQs
findings.publishedDate: unknown (page undated; references Resolution No. 500-1974)
findings.figure: Review tiers at 100 cy and 1,000 cy or 5 ft cuts/fills; 6 ft fence building-permit line
findings.bearsOn: Fence and hillside work pricing in Portola Valley: a property-line fence, the most common kind, needs a permit even at 4 ft, and compacted gravel counts as impervious surface, which affects patio and path design math.
findings.caveat: A 50-cubic-yard SDP trigger appearing in secondary code summaries was not verified on the fetched town page; confirm the exact trigger in PVMC Ch. 15.12 before quoting it.

findings.claim: Woodside requires a building permit for any retaining wall over 4 feet in height measured from the bottom of the footing to the top of the wall, or supporting a surcharge regardless of height, citing CBC 105.2 (Building 4) and CRC R105.2 (Building 3); free-standing walls that fall under the building-permit threshold may still need Planning Department approval.
findings.quote: Retaining walls that are over 4 feet (1219 mm) in height measured from the bottom of the footing to the top of the wall ... or supporting a surcharge
findings.sourceName: Town of Woodside, Retaining Wall Submittal Requirements Checklist
findings.publishedDate: unknown (page undated; fetched 2026-08-15)
findings.geography: Woodside, CA (rule derives from statewide CBC/CRC exemption thresholds, so the same baseline applies in GMZ's other towns absent local amendment)
findings.figure: 4 ft from bottom of footing; any height with surcharge
findings.bearsOn: Hardscape estimating: the 4 ft measurement is from the bottom of the footing, not the exposed face, so a wall that looks like 3 ft can still need a permit, and any wall holding back a slope or driveway (surcharge) needs one at any height.
findings.caveat: The Planning Department approval path for sub-threshold free-standing walls is stated on this page but its exact scope (fences, gates, wall heights by zone) was not detailed there.

findings.claim: Redwood City requires a building permit for all work not exempted by CBC 105.2 and names fences 7 feet tall and under among typical exempt residential items, directing applicants to CBC 105.2 for the full exemption list.
findings.quote: typical residential items such as fences 7' tall and under, painting, flooring, and similar finish work ... Please review the entirety of CBC 105.2 for all work exempt from permits.
findings.sourceName: City of Redwood City, Building FAQs
findings.publishedDate: unknown (page undated; FAQ text references the 2019 California Codes, suggesting it predates the current code cycle)
findings.figure: 7 ft fence building-permit exemption
findings.bearsOn: Fence line pricing in GMZ's home town: standard 6 ft fencing needs no building permit, but zoning height limits in setback areas apply separately from the building-permit exemption.
findings.caveat: The building-permit exemption is not a zoning clearance; Redwood City's R-district fence standards govern allowed heights by location on the lot and were not fetched. The FAQ's reference to the 2019 California Codes means the page may not reflect the current code edition, though the fence exemption in CBC 105.2 has been stable across editions.

findings.claim: Redwood City Municipal Code Section 32.105 bars transacting any business in the city without a Business License Tax Certificate, explicitly including self-employed persons and independent contractors; out-of-town businesses with under $50,000 of Redwood City revenue pay a flat rate equivalent to one full-time employee plus base tax and the state CASp fee, payment is due July 1 (delinquent after July 31), and delinquency carries a 10% per month penalty to a 100% maximum plus a $150 excess delinquency penalty for each prior year.
findings.quote: no person shall transact or operate any business in the City of Redwood City until a Business License Tax Certificate is obtained ... Self-employed persons and independent contractors are also required to obtain a Business License Tax Certificate.
findings.sourceName: City of Redwood City, Business License Tax Frequently Asked Questions
findings.publishedDate: unknown (page undated; fetched 2026-08-15)
findings.figure: Due July 1, delinquent after July 31; 10%/month penalty to 100% plus $150 per prior year; $50,000 out-of-town revenue threshold
findings.bearsOn: GMZ's compliance baseline in its home city, and a template for the unanswered question: each of the other nine towns likely has an equivalent rule for out-of-town contractors that this study did not verify.
