findings.caveat: The out-of-town flat-rate detail describes businesses based elsewhere working in Redwood City; GMZ, based in Redwood City, pays under the resident schedule. The other nine towns' license rules were not checked.

findings.claim: Federal civilian procurement caps the fee for production and delivery of design documents at 6 percent of estimated construction cost, and the cap applies only to that narrow production slice of A/E services, not to the full scope (studies, preliminary engineering, construction-phase support are outside the cap).
findings.quote: For architect-engineer services for public works or utilities, the contract price or the estimated cost and fee for production and delivery of designs, plans, drawings, and specifications shall not exceed 6 percent of the estimated cost of construction of the public work or utility, excluding fees.
findings.sourceName: FAR 15.404-4(c)(4)(i)(B), Acquisition.gov (implementing 10 U.S.C. 3322(b) and 41 U.S.C. 3905)
findings.publishedDate: current FAR text as fetched 2026-08-15
findings.figure: 6 percent of estimated construction cost
findings.bearsOn: The design-agreement fee percentage and the FAQ answer about design fees: the oft-quoted federal 6 percent is a cap on drawings-production only, on public works vastly larger than a Peninsula residence, so it is not a comparable ceiling for GMZ's full design service.
findings.caveat: Applies to public works or utilities at federal scale; the capped scope is much narrower than a residential design engagement that includes site analysis, client meetings, MWELO documentation and permit support. Misreading 6 percent as 'what design costs' understates every published full-service curve. Audit note: quote re-verified verbatim against the raw acquisition.gov page 2026-08-15, and the paragraph path (c)(4)(i)(B) confirmed in the raw HTML under '(c) Contracting officer responsibilities'.

findings.claim: Congress raised the Department of Defense statutory design-production fee cap from 6 percent to 10 percent of estimated project cost (Pub. L. 118-31, div. B, title XXVIII, section 2881(a), NDAA FY2024, enacted December 22, 2023, amending 10 U.S.C. 7540, 8612 and 9540), implemented in DFARS 236.606-70 by a final rule at 89 FR 53502 (June 27, 2024, DFARS Case 2024-D019, effective date delayed to September 16, 2024) — a legislative acknowledgment that 6 percent had become too low even on very large military construction projects.
findings.quote: The fee for any service under this section may not be more than 10 percent of the estimated cost, as determined by the Secretary, of the project to which it applies.
findings.sourceName: 10 U.S.C. 7540(b) (Army; parallel provisions at 8612 and 9540), U.S. House Office of the Law Revision Counsel; implemented in DFARS 236.606-70, Acquisition.gov
findings.publishedDate: statute amended December 22, 2023 (Pub. L. 118-31 sec. 2881(a)); DFARS final rule June 27, 2024, effective September 16, 2024; both texts fetched or corroborated 2026-08-15
findings.geography: United States (Army, Navy, Air Force contracts)
findings.figure: 10 percent of the project's estimated cost (raised from 6 percent)
findings.bearsOn: Defending a design fee above the folk '6 percent': the trend in published federal caps is upward, and the cap still covers only design-document production on projects orders of magnitude larger than GMZ's.
findings.caveat: Audit upgrade: the statute text and its amendment note ('Pub. L. 118-31 substituted 10 percent for 6 percent') were fetched directly from uscode.house.gov, and the current DFARS 236.606-70 text confirming 10 percent was fetched from acquisition.gov, so the core fact no longer rests on search snippets. The Federal Register rule text itself remains unfetched (bot-blocked); the 89 FR 53502 citation, June 27, 2024 date and September 16, 2024 effective date come from federalregister.gov result metadata. Military construction scale does not transfer to residential work.

findings.claim: Federal law requires design services to be procured on qualifications, with price negotiated afterward at a fair and reasonable level — the federal government's own policy is that design is not selected on price.
findings.quote: The policy of the Federal Government is to publicly announce all requirements for architectural and engineering services and to negotiate contracts for architectural and engineering services on the basis of demonstrated competence and qualification for the type of professional services required and at fair and reasonable prices.
findings.sourceName: 40 U.S.C. 1101 (Brooks Act policy), U.S. House Office of the Law Revision Counsel
findings.publishedDate: recodified Aug 21, 2002 (Pub. L. 107-217); originally added by Pub. L. 92-582, Oct 27, 1972
findings.bearsOn: How GMZ positions the paid design step in client conversations and the portfolio's design-services page: lead with qualifications and scope, present the percentage as the negotiated compensation for a defined scope, mirroring the federal model.
findings.caveat: Governs federal agencies, not private residential clients; it is a framing anchor, not a fee benchmark. Audit note: quote verified verbatim against uscode.house.gov 2026-08-15.

findings.claim: Washington State's published A/E fee schedule sets full basic-services design fees (design-bid-build columns) at its smallest tabulated project size, $1,000,000 MACC, of 12.09 percent (Schedule A, complex), 10.65 percent (Schedule B, whose building-type list includes 'Residences') and 9.21 percent (Schedule C, simple), falling to 6.86/5.89/4.91 percent at $100,000,000 — a published curve in which the percentage rises steadily as project size falls.
findings.quote: The actual contracts for basic services payable to the A/E shall be a negotiated fixed amount or percentage of the maximum allowable construction cost (MACC) of the projects, not including fees, licenses, permits, sales taxes, contingencies, and change orders caused by A/E errors or omissions or change orders which do not require design consultant services.
findings.sourceName: Washington State Office of Financial Management, 2025-27 Capital Budget Instructions, Chapter 9: A&E Fee Guidelines and Fee Schedule (basis: 2014 OFM-coordinated study with 2022 update involving the Washington Council of the AIA, ACEC of Washington and state agencies)
findings.publishedDate: June 2024, effective July 1, 2025
findings.sampleSize: guideline derived from a disclosed 2014 study and 2022 update, not a survey n
findings.bearsOn: The core bracket for GMZ's 10-15 percent design pricing: at the smallest size any state curve tabulates ($1M), the published full-service fee for residence-class work is already 10.65 percent, and OFM explicitly declines to extend the curve below $1M ('For projects under $1,000,000, the fee must be based on expected services and cost of work'), i.e., the percentage logic weakens, not strengthens, downward — GMZ's typical projects sit below every tabulated point.
findings.caveat: Public building projects in Washington, not California residential landscapes; the percentage buys full basic services including bidding and construction administration (see phase-split finding). Below $1M the guideline abandons the curve entirely rather than publishing higher percentages. Audit note: all six percentages, the verbatim quote, the under-$1M language, and the placement of 'Residences' in Schedule B (confirmed by column coordinates in the PDF) verified 2026-08-15; the table also carries separate, slightly different GC/CM columns — the cited figures are the design-bid-build columns.

findings.claim: In Washington's published basic-services fee, the design phases (schematic design 18 + design development 20 + construction document 31) account for 69 percent of the fee, while bidding (2), construction (27) and project closeout (2) account for 31 percent — so a design-only engagement corresponds to roughly two-thirds of any full-service fee percentage.
findings.sourceName: Washington State OFM, 2025-27 Capital Budget Instructions, Chapter 9 (Percent of Basic Services Fee breakdown)
findings.publishedDate: June 2024, effective July 1, 2025
findings.figure: Schematic design 18%, design development 20%, construction document 31%, bidding 2%, construction 27%, project closeout 2% of the basic services fee
findings.bearsOn: Making an honest comparison in GMZ's design-fee rationale: GMZ's design agreement is design-only (construction is a separate contract), so the comparable published number is about 0.69 x the full-service curve — roughly 7.3 percent of MACC at $1M for residence-class work (derived arithmetic, not a published figure) — before applying the small-project and existing-conditions premiums that published schedules acknowledge.
findings.caveat: The 7.3 percent is a derivation from two published numbers, stated as such; the 69/31 split itself is the published finding (the document labels the 27 percent phase 'Construction', i.e., construction-phase services). GMZ's design step may also include services (planting design detail, MWELO documentation) the OFM phases do not itemize. Audit note: all six phase percentages verified in the PDF 2026-08-15.

findings.claim: Washington's fee guideline allows remodel-project fees to be increased 'by up to three percent' above the schedule for basic services, citing existing-conditions factors (age and character of the building, availability and accuracy of existing plans, extent of program revisions), and it lists the 'Landscape Consultant' as a specialty consultant outside A/E basic services whose cost is additional to the curve, with specialty consultants normally capped at 50 percent of the basic A/E fee.
findings.quote: Generally, when program changes are significant or, if warranted by other conditions, fees noted under those schedules may be increased by up to three percent for basic services.
findings.sourceName: Washington State OFM, 2025-27 Capital Budget Instructions, Chapter 9 (Remodel design; specialty consultants list)
findings.publishedDate: June 2024, effective July 1, 2025
findings.figure: up to three percent above schedule for remodels (source wording; read in context as roughly 3 points on the schedule percentage, but the document does not say 'percentage points'); specialty consultants normally not greater than 50% of the basic A/E fee
findings.bearsOn: Two GMZ points: (1) renovation of an existing landscape (the normal Peninsula case — mature plantings, unknown irrigation, existing hardscape) is the published premium case, not the base case; (2) even inside a building fee, landscape design is priced as an addition to the curve, so a landscape-specific design fee is not bounded by the building curve.
findings.caveat: Audit correction: the source text says 'increased by up to three percent', not 'three percentage points'; because the fees being increased are themselves schedule percentages, the percentage-point reading is the natural one, but it is an interpretation, so quote the source wording if this is ever cited publicly. The premium is written for building remodels; the landscape-consultant classification reflects building-project scope allocation, not a statement about residential landscape design pricing. Quote and 50% cap sentence verified verbatim 2026-08-15.

findings.claim: Delaware's published state A/E fee schedule, in its smallest tabulated bracket (up to $500,000 construction cost, above a 'to be negotiated' floor at $100,000), sets full basic-services fees of 7.5-9.0 percent for new construction and 9.5-13.0 percent for renovation depending on complexity schedule; the renovation premium is 2-4 percentage points in that smallest bracket and narrows to 1-2 points at the largest tabulated bracket (up to $15,000,000), and the schedule reverts to 'to be negotiated' both below $100,000 and above $15,000,000.
findings.sourceName: Delaware Division of Facilities Management, Architectural & Engineering Fee Schedule (fees cover all basic services per AIA Document B101-2017 including construction administration)
findings.publishedDate: unknown (page undated; references AIA B101-2017; fetched 2026-08-15)
findings.figure: $100K-$500K bracket: 7.5%-9.0% new, 9.5%-13.0% renovation; renovation premium 2-4 points there, 1-2 points at the $15M bracket; under $100K and over $15M: negotiated
findings.bearsOn: The closest published bracket to GMZ's actual project sizes: at $100K-$500K construction, a state government pays up to 13 percent for full-service design on complex renovation work — placing GMZ's 10-15 percent design fee for small, complex, existing-site residential work inside the published public-sector band rather than above it. The premium narrowing with size also supports the small-project-premium argument: the renovation surcharge is largest exactly where GMZ operates.
findings.caveat: Audit correction: the original claim that renovation runs 2-4 points above new 'in every bracket' was false — at the $10M and $15M brackets the premium is 1.0-2.5 points (e.g., Schedule C at $15M: 6.5 vs 5.5). Smallest-bracket and largest-bracket values were confirmed by two independent fetch passes that agreed; mid-bracket values rest on a single extraction pass. The page carries no date, so currency is unverified; building projects, and the percentage includes construction-phase services (a design-only comparison should be scaled down, then adjusted back up for the sub-$100K sizes where Delaware itself abandons the schedule).

findings.claim: Caltrans reported preliminary engineering (all project development from project study report through construction contract award) at 19.7 percent of contract allotments and right-of-way capital for STIP projects awarded FY 2012-13, a 19.4 percent three-year average (FY 2010-11: 19.3%, FY 2011-12: 18.9%), against a Government Code target that the three-year average not exceed 20 percent.
findings.quote: According to the Government Code, the average cost of P.E. for the report year and two previous years shall not exceed the 20 percent target.
findings.sourceName: Caltrans, FY 2012-13 Annual Project Delivery Report to the California State Legislature (reporting under Government Code sections 14524.16 and 14525.5)
findings.publishedDate: report covers FY 2012-13; accessible PDF created July 30, 2019 per file metadata
findings.figure: 19.7% (FY 2012-13); 19.4% three-year average; statutory target < 20%; $3,394.6M construction and $657.6M PE over three years
findings.sampleSize: all programmed STIP projects awarded FY 2010-11 through FY 2012-13 ($3,394.6M construction, $657.6M PE over three years)
findings.bearsOn: California's own legislature accepts pre-construction engineering costing just under 20 percent of construction on public projects — a state-specific upper anchor showing GMZ's 10-15 percent design fee is well inside what California government itself pays for pre-construction work.
findings.caveat: PE here includes environmental clearance, right-of-way engineering and departmental overhead, a broader scope than a residential landscape design contract; highway projects do not transfer to residential scale, and the figure is what delivery costs the state, not a negotiated design fee. The data is FY 2012-13 era; use it as a historical statutory-target anchor, not a current statistic — newer annual reports were not audited. Audit note: all figures and the quote verified verbatim in the PDF 2026-08-15.

findings.claim: University research on North Carolina DOT projects let 2001-2009 found a mean preliminary-engineering cost ratio of 27.8 percent of estimated construction cost across 461 bridge projects (95% CI 26.0-29.6%) and 11.7 percent across 188 roadway projects, and reported that the most frequent PE budgeting percentage cited in the literature is ten percent of estimated construction costs, with a 25-DOT survey (WSDOT 2002) averaging 10.3 percent and ranging 4-20 percent.
findings.sourceName: Liu, Hummer, Rasdorf (North Carolina State University) and Hollar (East Carolina University), 'Preliminary Engineering Cost Trends for Highway Projects,' FHWA/NC/2010-10, NCDOT Research and Development Group
findings.publishedDate: October 21, 2011
findings.figure: 27.8% mean PE ratio (461 bridge projects); 11.7% (188 roadway projects); literature mode 10%; DOT survey mean 10.3%, range 4-20% (n=25)
findings.sampleSize: 461 bridge projects and 188 roadway projects (NCDOT, let 2001-2009); DOT survey n=25 (WSDOT 2002)
findings.bearsOn: Bracketing GMZ's percentage: technically complex projects (bridges) carry design/engineering shares near 28 percent, and the general planning figure across DOTs centers on 10 percent — so 10-15 percent for complex small-site design is between the general-case center and the complex-case mean in disclosed-sample research.
findings.caveat: PE includes planning and environmental work beyond design drawings; public infrastructure, 2001-2009 data, and figures are agency delivery costs rather than fees a client pays a designer. Audit note: every figure, the author affiliations and the October 21, 2011 report date verified in the PDF 2026-08-15; the 10.3%/4-20%/n=25 figures are the report's account of the 2002 WSDOT survey, not the authors' own sample.

findings.claim: A published cost curve derived from 30 completed Virginia DOT roadway projects (updated with 135 more for statewide verification; a parallel bridge curve from 23 projects) found preliminary-engineering cost ratios of 8 to 20 percent of construction cost and that the percentage is inversely related to construction cost — the disclosed-provenance version of 'small projects carry higher design percentages.'
findings.quote: The resulting ratio of PE costs to construction costs ranged from eight to twenty percent.  PE costs were found to be inversely related to construction costs.
findings.sourceName: FHWA/NC/2010-10 final report (NC State University for NCDOT), summarizing the VDOT estimating-tool studies (Kyte et al. 2004a, 2004b)
findings.publishedDate: October 21, 2011 (summarizing 2004 VDOT studies)
findings.figure: 8 to 20 percent of construction cost, inversely related to project size
findings.sampleSize: 30 completed VDOT roadway projects, curve updated with 135 additional projects; bridge curve from 23 projects
findings.bearsOn: The single most useful defensive point for GMZ's fee page and FAQ: every published curve found (WA OFM schedule, Delaware brackets, VDOT curve) rises as project size falls, so comparing a small residential design fee to percentages quoted for large projects is a category error the sources themselves warn against.
findings.caveat: Highway PE, not landscape design; the 20 percent upper end occurs at the small end of public roadway projects, which are still larger than most residential landscape jobs — the published curves simply stop before reaching GMZ's project sizes. Audit note: quote verified verbatim in the PDF 2026-08-15; this is the NC report's secondhand summary of the VDOT studies, which were not fetched directly.

findings.claim: The Chinowsky (Univ. of Colorado) and Kingsley (Georgia Tech) QBS study distributed by ACEC/APWA (2009), analyzing 41 predominantly public design-bid-build projects across 23 states, found change-order cost growth of 3 percent of final construction cost on QBS-procured projects versus an industry average the report characterizes as accepted to be about 10 percent, with construction schedule growth of 8.7 percent versus an ~10 percent industry average and an average design fee in the sample of $441,500 — evidence that qualified design earns back multiples of any plausible fee difference in avoided construction cost growth.
findings.sourceName: QBS Canada publication hosted by the Ontario Association of Architects (written by Ben Shelton, edited by Cal Harrison), 'Qualifications-Based Selection (QBS): Best Practice for Architecture, Engineering and Construction Management/General Contractor Procurement in Canada', reporting Chinowsky & Kingsley, 'An Analysis of Issues Pertaining to Qualifications-Based Selection' with page-level citations (pp. 20-21)
findings.publishedDate: August 2018 (underlying study 2009 per external corroboration; the QBS Canada report's footnotes cite the ACEC-hosted PDF without a year)
findings.figure: 3% cost growth (QBS) vs ~10% accepted industry average; schedule growth 8.7% vs ~10%; average design fee $441,500
findings.sampleSize: 41 predominantly public design-bid-build projects in 23 states
findings.bearsOn: Reframing what GMZ's design fee buys in proposals and the FAQ: the defensible argument is not 'everyone charges 10-15 percent' but 'a 7-point swing in construction cost growth dwarfs a few points of design fee' — the Brooks Act logic applied at residential scale.
findings.caveat: Primary study PDF (acec.ca) was not fetchable (403); all figures verified 2026-08-15 in the QBS Canada report text, which cites the study by page number, and the report itself says the ~10 percent industry-average baseline is 'accepted to be' the average, i.e., a characterization, not a measured control group. n=41 is small, projects are public and far larger than residential work. The 2009 date of the underlying study is corroborated by ACEC-ecosystem sources found in search, not by the report's own footnotes.

findings.claim: The DOJ obtained antitrust consent decrees against the AIA in 1972 (eliminating its fee schedule, in place since the 1860s, and its restrictions on competitive bidding) and again in 1990 (after the president of AIA Chicago circulated fee-setting documents, prohibiting architects from discussing fees with one another) — legal history consistent with the observed absence of any association-published 'industry standard' design-fee percentage.
findings.sourceName: Chris Gannon, AIA (principal, Shams Gannon Architecture), 'Opinion: Antitrust Law and the Remaking of the Profession,' Texas Architect Magazine, Vol. 76 Issue 2
findings.bearsOn: Explains Study 001's 'folklore' result and disciplines GMZ's own copy: the site and proposals should never claim an 'industry standard percentage' exists — the defensible framing is GMZ's published scope for a stated fee, benchmarked against government fee schedules (which are publications by buyers, not seller price-fixing).
findings.caveat: Audit correction: the original claim asserted the decrees are 'why' no association including ASLA publishes a fee percentage — that causal extension to ASLA is the researcher's inference, not in the source, and is restated here as consistency, not causation. Trade-press tier; DOJ primary documents (justice.gov) returned 401/403 and the decree language could not be quoted verbatim. The 1972/1990 decree facts, the 1860s fee-schedule vintage and the AIA Chicago trigger were verified in the fetched article 2026-08-15.

findings.claim: The best university-extension statement found on residential landscape design pricing says only that 'Some professionals charge by the hour, while others charge by the project,' with no percentages — university and extension sources validate the fee-structure taxonomy but publish no fee levels for residential landscape design.
findings.sourceName: University of Florida IFAS Extension, Florida-Friendly Landscaping program, 'Hiring a Design Professional' (FFL Minute radio transcript, Episode #169)
findings.publishedDate: October 22, 2020

findings.claim: The California Director of Finance certified on July 31, 2026 that the statewide minimum wage rises 2.99 percent, from the current $16.90 to $17.40 per hour for all employers on January 1, 2027, based on the U.S. CPI-W averaging period July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026.
findings.quote: This year, the Department of Finance calculates the average U.S. CPI-W for the 12-month period from July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026 increased by 2.99 percent compared to the 12-month period from July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025. As a result, pursuant to section 1182.12(c), the minimum wage shall increase by 2.99 percent to $17.40 per hour and shall be implemented for all employers on January 1, 2027.
findings.sourceName: California Department of Finance, Minimum Wage Increase, Director of Finance Determination and Certification (letter signed /s/ Joe Stephenshaw, Director)
findings.bearsOn: The maintenance renewal escalator: labor floor steps +2.99% on 2027-01-01, a known-in-advance input for any renewal priced before January.
findings.caveat: Audit 2026-08-15: PDF fetched and text extracted; letter date, signer, quote (verbatim), both wage figures, the 2.99 percent, and the CPI-W averaging periods all verified against the document. Corroborated by DIR News Release 2026-66 (dated Aug 13, 2026, fetched: 'California's statewide minimum wage will increase to $17.40 per hour' Jan 1, 2027; also states the 2027 exempt salary threshold of $72,384). The DIR minimum wage FAQ (fetched; page marked December 2025) still shows only $16.90 and does not yet mention $17.40; the FAQ lags the certification. Local ordinances can exceed the state floor; several Peninsula cities set their own minimum wages, which were not pulled in this study.

findings.claim: Labor Code 1182.12(c) sets the annual minimum wage escalator as the lesser of 3.5 percent and the change in the non-seasonally-adjusted U.S. CPI-W (July-June average over prior July-June average), rounded to the nearest ten cents, calculated by the Director of Finance on or before August 1 and effective the following January 1, with no decrease if CPI is negative.
findings.quote: The calculation shall increase the minimum wage by the lesser of 3.5 percent and the rate of change in the averages of the most recent July 1 to June 30, inclusive, period over the preceding July 1 to June 30, inclusive, period for the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics nonseasonally adjusted United States Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (U.S. CPI-W). The result shall be rounded to the nearest ten cents ($0.10). Each adjusted minimum wage increase calculated under this subdivision shall take effect on the following January 1.
findings.sourceName: California Labor Code section 1182.12 (Stats. 2016, Ch. 4, SB 3), official text at leginfo.legislature.ca.gov
findings.publishedDate: last amended Stats. 2016, Ch. 4 (SB 3), effective 2017-01-01
findings.figure: cap 3.5%; rounding $0.10; calc by Aug 1; effective Jan 1
findings.bearsOn: Escalation clause architecture: the state's own escalator (lesser-of formula, defined averaging window, cap, rounding, announcement date) is a directly copyable drafting pattern, and its Aug 1 announcement date means each January's floor is knowable before fall renewal notices go out.
findings.caveat: Audit 2026-08-15: leginfo fetched; the lesser-of-3.5-percent phrase, the $0.10 rounding rule, the following-January-1 effective date, the August 1 calculation deadline, and the no-decrease-on-negative-CPI provision were all confirmed against the section text, and the amendment history (Stats. 2016, Ch. 4, Sec. 3, SB 3) matches. Quote is assembled from the operative sentences of subdivision (c); the subdivision also provides that on a negative CPI 'there shall be no increase or decrease in the minimum wage.' The statute uses national CPI-W, not the Bay Area index, so GMZ's statutory labor floor and a Bay Area CPI clause move on different indexes.

findings.claim: BLS series CUUR0000SEHP02, 'Gardening and lawncare services in U.S. city average, all urban consumers, not seasonally adjusted' (Dec 1997=100), stood at 344.925 in July 2026 versus 307.218 in July 2025, a 12.3 percent 12-month increase (May-over-May: +10.8 percent).
findings.sourceName: BLS series CUUR0000SEHP02, data.bls.gov timeseries page; values cross-checked against the BLS Public Data API v2 (api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v2/timeseries/data/)
findings.publishedDate: retrieved 2026-08-15; latest observation July 2026
findings.bearsOn: Choice of escalator index: this is the trade-specific series Study 001 pointed at, and its current 12-month print (12.3%) versus SF all-items (3.8%) quantifies how much index choice matters in the renewal clause.
findings.caveat: Audit 2026-08-15: series title, Dec 1997=100 base period, and every cited value re-verified from two independent BLS routes (timeseries page and API): Jul 2026 344.925, Jul 2025 307.218 (+12.27% = +12.3%), May 2026 329.081, May 2025 296.976 (+10.8%). The sources return only scattered 2025 months (May, July, September) and October 2025 is footnoted 'Data unavailable due to the 2025 lapse in appropriations,' so the +12.3% print cannot be cross-checked against a full run of adjacent months. It is a national, not-seasonally-adjusted consumer-services index and is far more volatile than all-items CPI; using it as a sole escalator peg would have produced a double-digit increase this year that Peninsula clients would likely reject.

findings.claim: BLS series CUURS49BSA0, San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward all-items CPI-U (not seasonally adjusted), stood at 369.913 in June 2026 versus 356.460 in June 2025, a 3.8 percent 12-month increase, matching the 3.8 percent BLS states in its San Francisco area CPI release for the 12 months ending June 2026.
findings.quote: The San Francisco area all items CPI-U increased 3.8 percent for the 12 months ending in June.
findings.sourceName: BLS Public Data API v2, series CUURS49BSA0; corroborated by BLS West region San Francisco area CPI news release (www.bls.gov/regions/west/news-release/consumerpriceindex_sanfrancisco.htm)
findings.publishedDate: retrieved 2026-08-15; latest observation June 2026
findings.geography: San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward, CA metro area (Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, San Francisco, San Mateo counties)
findings.bearsOn: The default escalator peg for a maintenance renewal clause: the local all-items index a client will accept, currently running just above the 2.99% statewide minimum wage step.
findings.caveat: Audit 2026-08-15: API values re-fetched and verified (Jun 2026 369.913 / Jun 2025 356.460 = +3.77%, rounds to +3.8%), and the news release's stated 3.8 percent confirmed verbatim; a quote field was added from that release. Recent 12-month changes recomputed from retrieved values: Feb 2026 +2.5%, Apr 2026 +3.8%, Jun 2026 +3.8%. The metro CPI covers the whole SF-Oakland-Hayward area (the release lists San Mateo County among the five covered counties, so it does include the Peninsula, but not Santa Clara County); BLS publishes no finer-grained index for San Mateo County alone.

findings.claim: The San Francisco area CPI is published bimonthly, with observations existing only for even-numbered months (February, April, June, August, October, December), and the August 2026 index is scheduled for release September 11, 2026.
findings.quote: The August 2026 Consumer Price Index for the San Francisco area is scheduled to be released on September 11, 2026.
findings.sourceName: BLS West Information Office, Consumer Price Index, San Francisco Area news release (June 2026 data)
findings.publishedDate: covers June 2026 data; release page fetched 2026-08-15
findings.figure: 6 prints/year (even months)
findings.bearsOn: Clause drafting mechanics: which month's index the renewal formula names, and when the annual renewal notice can be computed.
findings.caveat: Audit 2026-08-15: the scheduled-release quote verified verbatim. Precision fix: the release itself says only that the index 'is published bi-monthly'; the even-month pattern is established by the retrieved series data (CUURS49BSA0 observations exist only for Feb/Apr/Jun/Aug/Oct/Dec), not stated explicitly in the release. A renewal clause pegged to this index must reference an even month and allow roughly six weeks of publication lag; a clause naming an odd month (e.g. 'the January index') can never be satisfied.

findings.claim: BLS index publication can fail outright: for both CUUR0000SEHP02 and CUURS49BSA0 the October 2025 observation is footnoted 'Data unavailable due to the 2025 lapse in appropriations,' so an escalation clause pegged to a single named month's index needs a stated fallback.
findings.quote: Data unavailable due to the 2025 lapse in appropriations
findings.sourceName: BLS Public Data API v2, footnote code X on series CUUR0000SEHP02 and CUURS49BSA0
findings.publishedDate: footnote observed 2026-08-15 on the October 2025 reference period
findings.figure: Oct 2025 observation missing in both series
findings.bearsOn: Escalation clause drafting: include a fallback (e.g. 'the most recent published index' or a named substitute) for months BLS does not publish.
findings.caveat: Audit 2026-08-15: footnote re-fetched and verified verbatim on the October 2025 observation of both series (footnote code X, value '-'). The Los Gatos precedent illustrates the companion risk: its clause names a CPI area BLS restructured, leaving the contract pointing at an index title that no longer matches BLS publications.
