findings.claim: Under Business and Professions Code 17602 as amended, a consumer contract that renews automatically after an initial term of one year or longer requires a renewal reminder notice at least 15 and not more than 45 days before renewal, disclosing the product or service, the renewal frequency and charges, and how to cancel.
findings.quote: at least 15 days and not more than 45 days before the automatic renewal offer or continuous service offer renews
findings.sourceName: California Business and Professions Code section 17602, official text at leginfo.legislature.ca.gov
findings.publishedDate: last amended Stats. 2024, Ch. 515 (AB 2863), effective 2025-01-01
findings.figure: reminder window 15-45 days pre-renewal
findings.bearsOn: The annual renewal notice GMZ must send on auto-renewing maintenance agreements and the calendar slot in which the new-year price must be communicated.
findings.caveat: Audit 2026-08-15: the 15/45-day timing phrase re-verified verbatim against a fresh leginfo fetch, and the amendment history (Stats. 2024, Ch. 515, Sec. 2, AB 2863) confirmed. Applies to consumer contracts, which residential maintenance accounts are; it would not govern a commercial or HOA account. The reminder window pairs naturally with the escalator: the same annual notice can carry both the reminder and the computed CPI adjustment.

findings.claim: B&P 17602 requires that a consumer who accepted an automatic renewal online be able to terminate exclusively online, at will, without obstructing steps, including via a prominently located direct link or button.
findings.quote: Allow a consumer to terminate the automatic renewal or continuous service exclusively online, at will, and without engaging any further steps that obstruct or delay the consumer's ability to terminate. ... A prominently located direct link or button which may be located within either a customer account or profile, or within either device or user settings.
findings.sourceName: California Business and Professions Code section 17602, official text at leginfo.legislature.ca.gov
findings.publishedDate: last amended Stats. 2024, Ch. 515 (AB 2863), effective 2025-01-01
findings.bearsOn: How GMZ structures maintenance-agreement signup and the cancellation channel the agreement must name.
findings.caveat: Audit 2026-08-15: both quoted fragments re-verified against a second independent leginfo fetch, including the 'without engaging any further steps that obstruct or delay' language and the full link-or-button placement sentence; both match verbatim. The exclusively-online cancellation duty attaches when the consumer accepted the offer online. If GMZ signs maintenance agreements on paper or by emailed signature rather than through a website flow, the online-exclusive mechanism is not triggered, but a toll-free number, email address, or another cost-effective, timely and easy-to-use mechanism is still required. Subdivision lettering not independently verified beyond the fetched text.

findings.claim: B&P 17602 requires that before a material change to the terms of an accepted automatic renewal (a price escalation qualifies), the business provide a clear and conspicuous notice of the change plus cancellation information, in a manner capable of being retained by the consumer.
findings.quote: clear and conspicuous notice of the material change and provide information regarding how to cancel in a manner that is capable of being retained by the consumer
findings.sourceName: California Business and Professions Code section 17602, official text at leginfo.legislature.ca.gov
findings.publishedDate: last amended Stats. 2024, Ch. 515 (AB 2863), effective 2025-01-01
findings.bearsOn: Whether the escalator can operate silently: it should not; the annual notice should state the computed new price.
findings.caveat: Audit 2026-08-15: quote extended to the full statutory phrase, verified across two independent leginfo fetches; the retention language is 'in a manner that is capable of being retained by the consumer' and the claim wording was aligned to it. Even a formula-driven CPI increase changes the amount charged; the conservative reading is that each year's computed adjustment goes in the pre-renewal notice rather than being applied silently. Whether a pre-agreed formula escapes 'material change' is unsettled; drafting the annual notice to state the new dollar amount moots the question.

findings.claim: AB 2863 (Stats. 2024, Ch. 515, approved September 24, 2024) applies its amendments to the automatic renewal law to contracts entered into, amended, or extended on or after July 1, 2025, so every GMZ maintenance agreement renewing after that date is covered by the amended requirements.
findings.quote: The amendments made to this section by the act adding this subdivision shall only apply to a contract entered into, amended, or extended under this article on or after July 1, 2025.
findings.sourceName: AB 2863 (2023-2024), chaptered text at leginfo.legislature.ca.gov
findings.publishedDate: approved 2024-09-24 (Chapter 515)
findings.figure: operative 2025-07-01
findings.bearsOn: Compliance status of GMZ's existing ~24 recurring maintenance accounts as they roll over.
findings.caveat: Audit 2026-08-15: chaptered bill fetched; Chapter 515, September 24, 2024 approval, and the quoted July 1, 2025 applicability provision verified verbatim (the identical sentence appears in both Section 1 (17601) and Section 2 (17602) of the bill). Because an automatic renewal is an extension, legacy maintenance agreements do not stay grandfathered: each renewal cycle after July 1, 2025 pulls the contract into the amended regime.

findings.claim: The Town of Los Gatos's executed landscape services agreement with Brightview Landscape Services, Inc. (dated for identification June 21, 2022; term July 1, 2022 through June 30, 2027; year-one compensation capped at $175,772, five-year base amount $878,860) contains an upward-only annual CPI escalator pegged to a named metro CPI-U index with a floor at the base amount.
findings.quote: Compensation for year one shall not exceed $175,772. Compensation for future years shall be adjusted upward annually for the remaining term of this agreement by the change, if any, in the San Francisco-Oakland-San Jose Metropolitan Area Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers, all items (CPI). The adjustment shall be based upon the CPI published on December 31 of the preceding year. If the CPI indicates a downward adjustment, compensation will remain at the base amount.
findings.sourceName: Town of Los Gatos, Agreement for Services with Brightview Landscape Services, Inc. (public record, town document portal)
findings.publishedDate: 2022-06-21 (dated for identification)
findings.figure: year-one cap $175,772; 5-year term; total base $878,860; upward-only annual CPI adjustment
findings.bearsOn: Drafting precedent for the maintenance renewal escalator: proof that public agencies in the region accept automatic upward-only CPI adjustment, and a caution on index-naming precision.
findings.caveat: Audit 2026-08-15: PDF fetched and text extracted; the CPI clause verified verbatim (section 2.6), the June 21, 2022 identification date, the July 1, 2022 to June 30, 2027 term, the $175,772 year-one cap, and an additional detail the original finding omitted: the agreement states a total five-year base amount of $878,860 'prior to any increase adjustments for CPI.' Two drafting lessons, one positive and one negative: the upward-only ratchet with a base-amount floor is client-tested language, but the clause names the 'San Francisco-Oakland-San Jose' CPI area, which does not match the current BLS area title (San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward, series CUURS49BSA0), and no CPI 'published on December 31' exists since the SF index prints only for even months with a lag. A GMZ clause should name the exact series ID and a fallback. Public-agency scale (six-figure annual contract, competitively bid, prevailing-wage work under Labor Code 1720 et seq.) differs from a residential account.

findings.claim: The City of Fairfield's executed landscape maintenance agreement with New Image Landscape Company for Landscaping and Lighting Maintenance District No. 13 (North Cordelia), initial term January 1, 2022 through December 31, 2023, permits up to two 24-month extension terms with a negotiated compensation adjustment capped at the June San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward CPI-W (not seasonally adjusted, all items), requiring mutual written agreement.
findings.quote: This Agreement may be extended for up to two (2) additional terms of up to twenty-four (24) months each term with the same terms and conditions including a negotiated compensation adjustment not to exceed the June San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (not seasonally adjusted for all items) upon mutual written Agreement of both parties.
findings.sourceName: City of Fairfield, Contractor Services Agreement with New Image Landscape Company, Landscaping and Lighting Maintenance District No. 13 - North Cordelia (public agenda attachment)
findings.publishedDate: unknown (execution date line blank in document; executed via DocuSign; initial term begins 2022-01-01)
findings.figure: adjustment cap: June SF-Oakland-Hayward CPI-W; extensions up to 2 x 24 months
findings.bearsOn: Alternative escalator architecture: cap-at-CPI-W with mutual agreement, and the case for aligning the contract index with the index that drives wage costs.
findings.caveat: Audit 2026-08-15: PDF fetched and text extracted; the extension/CPI clause (section 8, TERM) verified verbatim, and the January 1, 2022 to December 31, 2023 initial term confirmed. The audit adds identification the original finding lacked: the contractor is New Image Landscape Company (Fremont, CA) and the covered work is Landscaping and Lighting Maintenance District No. 13, North Cordelia. Notable for pegging to the June CPI-W print, the same index family and a similar summer reference point as the Labor Code 1182.12 minimum wage formula, so contract price and wage floor move on related measures. It is a cap-with-negotiation model, weaker for the contractor than Los Gatos's automatic adjustment. Solano County market, not the Peninsula.

findings.claim: Customers acquired through a bank's pay-per-referral program had a six-year customer lifetime value approximately 40 euros (about 16%) higher than demographically comparable nonreferred customers (nonreferred base 253 euros), rising to approximately 25% when their roughly 20 euro lower acquisition cost is included, implying about a 60% return over six years on the 25 euro referral reward.
findings.sourceName: Schmitt, Skiera & Van den Bulte, "Referral Programs and Customer Value," Journal of Marketing 75(1): 46-59
findings.figure: +16% CLV (EUR 40 on EUR 253 base); ~25% net of acquisition costs; ~60% ROI on EUR 25 reward
findings.sampleSize: Original sample 5,181 referred + 4,633 nonreferred customers acquired in 2006; purified analysis sample 9,495 after outlier deletion; tracked ~33 months, CLV projected over six years
findings.bearsOn: Whether GMZ formalizes a referral program and what a referral thank-you or reward is economically worth
findings.caveat: All figures verified verbatim in the full text on audit (40 euros, 253 euro base, 16%, 20 euro acquisition-cost gap, 25%, ~60% ROI on the 25 euro reward, sample counts). Single German retail bank, consumer accounts with EUR-scale margins; direction transfers to a four-person Peninsula design/build firm, magnitude does not. The paper itself warns the differential is not uniform: it was absent for low-margin customers and customers over 55, so a GMZ program should be selective, not blanket.

findings.claim: Referred customers' contribution margin advantage (7.6 cents/day, ~25% above the 30 cents/day nonreferred baseline, 27.74 euros/year) eroded by 8.4 cents/year and disappeared after about 857 days (~29 months), while their retention advantage (churn hazard ~18% lower after demographic controls; 33-month survival 82.0% vs 79.2%) showed no statistically significant erosion over time.
findings.sourceName: Schmitt, Skiera & Van den Bulte, "Referral Programs and Customer Value," Journal of Marketing 75(1): 46-59
findings.figure: +25% daily margin, gone by ~857 days (~29 months); churn hazard -18% [exp(-.198)-1]; 82.0% vs 79.2% retention at 33 months
findings.sampleSize: 9,495 customers (purified sample; fixed-effects margin model on 9,495 fixed-effects estimates)
findings.bearsOn: Why the durable payoff of a referred client is loyalty, not spend: supports steering referred design/build clients toward recurring maintenance accounts rather than expecting permanently larger projects
findings.caveat: Every figure verified verbatim in the full text on audit, including the erosion rate (23.1 cents per 1,000 days = 8.4 cents/year) and the 857-day calculation (.198/.000231). Banking relationship with continuous monthly margins; a design/build project is lumpier. The loyalty finding maps most cleanly to GMZ's recurring maintenance accounts. Note the -18% hazard effect is multiplicative on a small baseline hazard, which is why the absolute survival gap is only 2.8 points at 33 months.

findings.claim: Referred customers' churn hazard is about 40% lower than nonreferred customers only while their referrer remains a customer; once the referrer defects, the referred customer's churn hazard flips to about 280% higher than nonreferred, and the authors' stated management recommendation is to recruit referrers among customers acquired at least six months earlier who exhibit high margins and are unlikely to churn.
findings.sourceName: Van den Bulte, Bayer, Skiera & Schmitt, "How Customer Referral Programs Turn Social Capital into Economic Capital," Journal of Marketing Research 55(1): 132-146
findings.geography: Germany (same retail bank as the 2011 study)
findings.figure: -40% churn hazard while referrer stays [exp(-.48)-1]; +280% after referrer churns [exp(-.48+1.82)-1]
findings.sampleSize: 1,799 single-referral referrer-referral dyads (49% of all referrals acquired in the January-October 2006 window) + 3,663 randomly drawn nonreferred customers; observed 33 months (January 2006-September 2008)
findings.bearsOn: Which clients GMZ should ask for referrals (established, satisfied, long-tenure maintenance accounts) and why losing a referrer endangers the clients they brought in: retention calls to a referrer protect two relationships, not one
findings.caveat: Verified verbatim from extracted full text on audit, including both hazard calculations and the six-month recommendation sentence. Correction from the draft: referrals were acquired January-October 2006, not February-October. One bank, single-referral dyads only; the bank confirmed the included dyads are unrelated to margin or churn, but 51% of referrals in the window are excluded. In a Peninsula neighbor network the social-enrichment mechanism plausibly operates, but no home-services replication exists.

findings.claim: Word-of-mouth referrals showed a long-run elasticity of new-customer signups of 0.53, roughly 20 times the elasticity of the firm's marketing events (0.026) and 30 times that of media appearances (0.017), with WOM effects on signups remaining significantly different from zero for about three weeks versus a few days for traditional marketing; the authors compute an implied referral value of about 75 cents per year and explicitly frame it as an upper bound for incentive spending.
findings.sourceName: Trusov, Bucklin & Pauwels, "Effects of Word-of-Mouth Versus Traditional Marketing," Journal of Marketing 73(5): 90-102 (fetched copy is the April 2008 working-paper version, Robert H. Smith School WP RHS-06-060, hosted at UCLA)
findings.publishedDate: 2009-09 (published); fetched file dated 2008-04-24
findings.figure: Long-run WOM elasticity 0.53 vs 0.026 (events) and 0.017 (media); carryover ~3 weeks; ~USD 0.75/referral/year (explicit upper bound)
findings.sampleSize: 36 weeks of daily signup and referral data from one anonymous social networking site (2005)
findings.bearsOn: The evidence behind treating referrals as GMZ's primary acquisition channel ahead of paid media
findings.caveat: All figures verified in the extracted text on audit, including the upper-bound framing of the 75-cent figure. Note the URL serves the pre-publication working-paper version, not the typeset Journal of Marketing article; figures in the fetched version match the claim. A free, ad-funded social platform with electronically tracked invitations is structurally unlike hiring a contractor; take the direction (WOM outperforms paid, with longer carryover), not the ratios. The 75-cent figure is the platform's ad economics and does not transfer.

findings.claim: In applications at a telecommunications company and a financial services firm covering thousands of customers, the customers with the highest customer lifetime value were generally not the customers with the highest customer referral value, and the abstract states both companies reaped returns on marketing investments greater than 12-fold, more than double the normal marketing ROI for their industries.
findings.sourceName: Kumar, Petersen & Leone, "How Valuable Is Word of Mouth?," Harvard Business Review 85(10): 139-146
findings.figure: >12-fold reported marketing ROI from CLV+CRV targeting
findings.sampleSize: "Thousands of customers" at two firms; exact n not disclosed in the fetched record
findings.bearsOn: GMZ should ask its proven referrers for referrals, not just its biggest-budget clients: track who actually refers, separately from project size
findings.caveat: Re-verified on audit: the Penn State Pure record's abstract contains the >12-fold and double-industry-ROI language and the telecom/financial-services setting. HBR is practitioner literature, not peer review, and the full text remains paywalled; the figure rests on the abstract only. The peer-reviewed companion is the 2010 Journal of Marketing paper (separate finding).

findings.claim: Four field experiments with firms in financial services and retailing found that profitability from referral marketing is maximized by managing customers jointly on customer lifetime value and customer referral value and by targeting campaigns using the behavioral drivers of referral value, per the peer-reviewed abstract.
findings.sourceName: Kumar, Petersen & Leone, "Driving Profitability by Encouraging Customer Referrals: Who, When, and How," Journal of Marketing 74(5): 1-17
findings.sampleSize: Four field experiments; per-experiment n not disclosed in fetched abstract
findings.bearsOn: Design of any GMZ referral push: who gets asked and when
findings.caveat: Re-verified on audit: the fetched abstract matches the claim word for word in substance and contains no profit-lift percentage. The widely quoted 10-30% profit-lift figure for these experiments appears only in secondary summaries and could not be verified; treat any such magnitude as unverified. Full text paywalled.

findings.claim: The oldest peer-reviewed antecedent for a post-completion thank-you call is Carey, Clicque, Leighton & Milton (1976), 'A Test of Positive Reinforcement of Customers,' Journal of Marketing 40: 98-100, which Grant & Gino (2010, JPSP) cite among a number of experiments showing that when helpers are thanked by the beneficiaries of their help, they are more willing to help those beneficiaries again.
findings.sourceName: Carey, Clicque, Leighton & Milton (1976), Journal of Marketing 40: 98-100, as cited in Grant & Gino 2010, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 98(6): 946-955
findings.publishedDate: 1976 (original); 2010-06 (citing source, the one actually fetched)
findings.sampleSize: Not verifiable; the original two-page note is paywalled (Sage returned 403)
findings.bearsOn: The closest peer-reviewed support for GMZ's recommended 30-day post-completion thank-you/check-in call
findings.caveat: Corrected on audit: the draft claim's details (retail jewelry store, three scripted telephone-call conditions) do NOT appear in the fetched Grant & Gino text and are unverifiable from any fetched source, so they have been stripped from the claim. What the fetched source verifies is the citation itself (reference list confirms Journal of Marketing, 40, 98-100, 1976) and the sentence: 'A number of experiments have shown that when helpers are thanked by the beneficiaries of their help, helpers are more willing to help these beneficiaries again (Carey, Clicque, Leighton, & Milton, 1976; ...)'. The widely circulated ~70% purchase-increase figure is likewise unverified and deliberately not asserted. Support is qualitative direction only, via a citing source.

findings.claim: A meta-analysis of service-recovery studies found the cumulative mean effect of the service recovery paradox (a well-recovered failure producing higher satisfaction than no failure) significant and positive for satisfaction but nonsignificant for repurchase intentions, word of mouth, and corporate image.
findings.sourceName: de Matos, Henrique & Rossi, "Service Recovery Paradox: A Meta-Analysis," Journal of Service Research 10(1): 60-77
findings.geography: Multi-country pooled studies; moderator analysis covers hotel, restaurant, and other service categories
findings.figure: Positive significant cumulative effect on satisfaction; nonsignificant on repurchase intent, WOM, image
findings.sampleSize: Meta-analysis; study/effect-size count not disclosed in the fetched abstract (full text paywalled)
findings.bearsOn: Why the 30-day and six-month calls should actively surface problems: fixing a surfaced complaint restores satisfaction, but a failure well recovered cannot be counted on to generate more repurchase or referrals than doing the job right, so recovery is a floor, not a growth strategy
findings.caveat: Re-verified on audit: the fetched abstract states the satisfaction/repurchase/WOM/image split exactly as claimed, and confirms moderators (cross-sectional vs longitudinal design, student vs nonstudent subjects, service category) influence the satisfaction effect. Underlying pool is hospitality-heavy; no landscaping or contracting studies. Confidence is high for what the abstract states, but the effect-size magnitudes remain unverified behind the paywall.

findings.claim: Using a regression discontinuity around Yelp's half-star rounding thresholds, an extra half-star rating caused San Francisco restaurants to sell out 19 percentage points (49%) more frequently, with larger impacts when alternate information about the business is more scarce; restaurants without external accreditation (no Michelin star or Chronicle Top 100 listing) sold out 20-30 percentage points more frequently per extra half-star, while externally accredited restaurants showed no significant effect.
findings.sourceName: Anderson & Magruder, "Learning from the Crowd: Regression Discontinuity Estimates of the Effects of an Online Review Database," The Economic Journal 122(563): 957-989 (fetched copy is the author-hosted manuscript)
findings.figure: +19 percentage points (49%) sellout frequency per extra displayed half-star; 20-30 pp for restaurants without external accreditation, ~0 for accredited
findings.sampleSize: 328 San Francisco restaurants with matched Yelp and online-reservation data (full Yelp sample 3,953 restaurants); reservation availability recorded July-October 2010
findings.bearsOn: Why GMZ's review profile matters most exactly where it operates: the effect is strongest when the buyer has little other information, which is the position of a homeowner hiring an unfamiliar contractor
findings.caveat: Verified from extracted full text on audit. One word corrected: the abstract says 'alternate information', not 'alternative information'. The headline 19 pp figure is the 7:00 pm pooled estimate; 6:00 pm (11 pp) and 8:00 pm (15 pp) estimates are smaller and weaker. Restaurants are a frequent, low-ticket purchase; a landscape project is rare and high-ticket, so the buyer does more diligence beyond the star display. Fetched file is the author-hosted manuscript, not the journal typeset version.

findings.claim: A one-star increase in displayed Yelp rating leads to a 5-9 percent increase in restaurant revenue, and the effect is driven by independent restaurants; ratings do not affect restaurants with chain affiliation, consistent with online reviews substituting for traditional reputation.
findings.sourceName: Luca, "Reviews, Reputation, and Revenue: The Case of Yelp.com," Harvard Business School Working Paper 12-016
findings.publishedDate: 2011-09 (working paper; fetched copy is copyright 2011, 2016)
findings.figure: +5-9% revenue per one-star Yelp increase; no effect for chain-affiliated restaurants
findings.sampleSize: Yelp reviews (60,000+ covering ~70% of operational Seattle restaurants as of 2009) matched to Washington State Department of Revenue revenue records for all Seattle restaurants, 2003-2009
findings.bearsOn: The independent-business result is the transferable part for GMZ: reputation platforms matter precisely for independents without a brand, so systematically converting satisfied clients into reviews is channel-building, not vanity
findings.caveat: Verified from extracted full text on audit: the 5-9% figure, the independent-vs-chain split, and the WA Department of Revenue data source all appear verbatim. University working paper, never journal-published in this form (T1 under this study's rules as a university publication, but not peer-reviewed; the peer-reviewed cousin is Anderson & Magruder 2012). The draft's 'revised 2016-03' precision was not confirmable from the document, which shows only copyright 2011, 2016. Restaurant revenue dynamics do not translate into a landscaping revenue elasticity.

findings.claim: In a randomized field experiment with 2,000 customers of a Chinese online children's-apparel retailer on TMall, combining a financial incentive with a social-norm message nearly tripled the share of customers writing a review versus a 4% no-intervention baseline, and the resulting reviews were approximately 50% longer than the ~52-character (~10 word) control baseline; financial incentives mainly drove review volume while social-norm information had the greater effect on review length.
findings.sourceName: Burtch, Hong, Bapna & Griskevicius, "Stimulating Online Reviews by Combining Financial Incentives and Social Norms," Management Science 64(5): 2065-2082
findings.geography: China (field study); US (AMT replication and Amazon archival data)
findings.figure: Review authorship nearly tripled vs 4% baseline; review length +~50% vs ~52-character baseline
findings.sampleSize: 2,000 customers (field experiment, TMall children's-apparel retailer, China; incentive ¥10 ≈ US$1.50) + Amazon Mechanical Turk replication + archival Amazon review study
findings.bearsOn: How GMZ asks for reviews at the 30-day call: an ask that mentions that other clients have left reviews (norm) measurably improves response, and pairing a small gesture with the ask outperforms either alone
findings.caveat: Verified from extracted full text on audit, including footnotes 2 and 3 (4% baseline; ~52 English characters ≈ 10 words) and the sentiment result: the experiments showed no treatment-induced sentiment bias, but the paper's large-scale archival analysis of Amazon reviews 'does indicate that financial incentives lead to more positive reviews in that setting'. Yelp and Google prohibit incentivized reviews, so GMZ should use the norm message, not payment. E-commerce apparel in China; magnitudes do not transfer.

findings.claim: In a published CLV valuation framework applied to five firms, improving customer retention by 1% improves customer and firm value by 3-7% (retention elasticity 3-7), versus a margin elasticity of about 1 and an acquisition-cost elasticity of only 0.02-0.3; a 1% improvement in retention has almost five times greater impact on customer value than a comparable change in the discount rate.
findings.sourceName: Gupta, Lehmann & Stuart, "Valuing Customers," Journal of Marketing Research 41(1): 7-18 (fetched copy is the Columbia-hosted working-paper version)
findings.publishedDate: 2004-02 (published); fetched working-paper version undated on cover
findings.figure: Retention elasticity 3-7 vs margin ~1 vs acquisition cost 0.02-0.3; retention ~5x the impact of discount rate
findings.sampleSize: Five publicly traded firms: Capital One, Amazon, Ameritrade, eBay, E*Trade (quarterly public data through March 2002)
findings.bearsOn: The published framework for valuing GMZ's recurring maintenance accounts against one-time project clients: effort that keeps a recurring account (the six-month call) has several times the value leverage of equivalent effort shaving acquisition cost
findings.caveat: Verified verbatim on audit from the Columbia-hosted working paper: 'improving customer retention by 1% is likely to improve customer and firm value by 3-7%... margin elasticity is about 1 and acquisition elasticity is only 0.02-0.3... 1% improvement in retention has almost five times greater impact on customer value' (than discount rate). Subscription-style firms with huge customer bases; the elasticity ordering (retention > margin > acquisition) is the transferable insight, not the multiples.

findings.claim: The frequently quoted retention-profit multiplier traces to Bain/Reichheld consultancy analysis, whose fetchable form states: "In financial services, for example, a 5% increase in customer retention produces more than a 25% increase in profit," with return customers referring others explicitly listed among the mechanisms.
findings.sourceName: Reichheld, "Prescription for Cutting Costs," Bain & Company brief (lineage: Reichheld & Sasser, "Zero Defections," HBR 68(5): 105-111, 1990)
findings.publishedDate: 2001-10 (PDF creation date 2001-10-24 per metadata; cites Loyalty Rules!, Sept 2001)
findings.geography: United States, multi-industry consultancy client base
findings.figure: 5% retention increase -> >25% profit increase (financial services; consultancy analysis, method undisclosed)
findings.bearsOn: If GMZ's client-facing or internal documents quote the famous 5%-retention line, this is its honest provenance: consultancy analysis with undisclosed method, not peer-reviewed research; the peer-reviewed substitute is Gupta et al. 2004
findings.caveat: Verified verbatim on audit: the quoted sentence appears exactly in the fetched brief, which also states 'return customers refer others to your company' among the mechanisms. Publication date upgraded from 'unknown' to October 2001 based on PDF metadata. The original 1990 HBR industry-by-industry figures (bank branches, insurance brokerage, auto-service) remain paywalled and are not asserted as verified.

products.title: GMZ Landscaping Inc., One-Visit Counsel Brief: Design Agreement, Home Improvement Contract Coverage, Cancellation Rights, Plan License, Maintenance Contracts
products.body:
NOTICE ON THE NATURE OF THIS DOCUMENT

This brief assembles public statutory and regulatory texts, verbatim operative language, and precise questions for counsel. It contains no legal conclusions and no legal advice. It was prepared by a researcher so that counsel does not have to retrieve or verify the primary texts during the consultation. Every quotation below was verified against the cited official source on 2026-08-15 unless a caveat says otherwise. Where the research found nothing on a point, that negative result is stated expressly, because knowing what does not exist is part of what this brief delivers.

CLIENT FACT BASE

GMZ Landscaping Inc., a licensed California landscape contractor, CSLB license 636636, classification C-27, based in Redwood City, working residential properties on the San Francisco Peninsula (Redwood City, Atherton, Menlo Park, Palo Alto, Woodside, San Carlos, Belmont, Portola Valley, Los Altos, Hillsborough). Two lines of business: (1) residential design/build, in which design is sold as a separate paid step under its own signed agreement, priced as a share of anticipated construction cost, with construction under a second, later contract; and (2) approximately 24 recurring residential maintenance accounts, some auto-renewing. Contracts in both lines are ordinarily signed at the client's home, not at GMZ's place of business. The client base skews older; buyers 65 and over are common, especially in Atherton, Hillsborough and Woodside. A prior research study established the statutory frame: B&P 7159 contract contents, the 7159.5 downpayment cap, MWELO's documentation trigger at 500 square feet, and that a licensed landscape contractor may sign the MWELO design plan.

THE FIVE QUESTIONS

QUESTION 1. Is a paid design-only agreement within a C-27 licensee's authority under B&P 7027.5 and 5641.4, given that both statutes grant design authority only for work "to be performed and supervised by that contractor," and may the client lawfully take the finished plans to another builder? Commercial stake: GMZ sells design as a standalone paid product, and some clients will not build, or will build with someone else, so the whole design revenue line rests on this construction.

QUESTION 2. Is the standalone design agreement itself a "home improvement contract" under B&P 7151.2, via the 7151 and Civil Code 1689.5 services chain, and therefore subject to the 7159 content requirements and the 7159.5 downpayment cap? Commercial stake: this determines the required form of GMZ's design agreement, whether a design retainer is capped, and whether noncompliance exposes GMZ to discipline and unenforceability arguments on every design sale.

QUESTION 3. When exactly does the three-business-day (five-day for buyers 65 and older) right to cancel attach and start running, reconciling the purely locational trigger in B&P 7159(e)(6)(A) with CSLB's consumer guidance that adds a $25 price floor drawn from Civil Code 1689.5? Commercial stake: GMZ signs at kitchen tables, so nearly every contract carries the notice, and starting design work inside an unexpired cancellation window risks doing unpaid work or tainting the contract.

QUESTION 4. What limited-license language should the design agreement carry over the plan set, consistent with the "performed and supervised by that contractor" limit, the ban on the title "landscape architect" in B&P 5641.4 and 5640, and the line B&P 5641 draws for construction-level documents? Commercial stake: the plan license clause is where the Question 1 risk is either managed or aggravated, and title-related wording errors in the agreement or marketing carry misdemeanor exposure.

QUESTION 5. Does the recurring maintenance service agreement, or any single visit or ad-hoc repair above $750, fall inside the home improvement contract regime, and when can the service-and-repair form under B&P 7159.10 be used instead? Commercial stake: 24 recurring accounts are the stable half of the business, and using the wrong contract form on routine work either burdens every visit with 7159 formalities or leaves GMZ noncompliant on the larger ones.

QUESTION 1: ASSEMBLED TEXTS

B&P 7027.5(a), official text at leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, last amended Stats. 2012, Ch. 537 (AB 1750), verified current 2026-08-15:
"(a) A landscape contractor working within the classification for which the license is issued may design systems or facilities for work to be performed and supervised by that contractor."
Subdivision (e), verbatim: "Nothing in this section authorizes a landscape contractor to engage in or perform activities that require a license pursuant to the Professional Engineers Act (Chapter 7 (commencing with Section 6700))."

B&P 5641.4 (Landscape Architects Practice Act exemption), official text, last amended Stats. 2024, Ch. 482 (SB 1452), effective 2025-01-01, verified current 2026-08-15:
"A landscape contractor licensed under the statutes of this state, insofar as they work within the classification for which the license is issued, may design systems and facilities for work to be performed and supervised by that landscape contractor and is exempt from this chapter, except that a landscape contractor shall not use the title 'landscape architect' unless they hold a license as required under this chapter."
Note for counsel: the identical "performed and supervised by that contractor" formula appears in both the Contractors' State License Law and the LA Practice Act; the two can be read in pari materia. Section 5641.4 was amended effective 2025, so older secondary summaries may quote superseded wording.

B&P 5615 (definition of the practice of landscape architecture), official text, verified current 2026-08-15:
"A person who practices landscape architecture within the meaning and intent of this article is a person who offers or performs professional services, for the purpose of landscape preservation, development and enhancement, such as consultation, investigation, reconnaissance, research, planning, design, preparation of drawings, construction documents and specifications, and responsible construction observation."
Everything GMZ's paid design step produces appears to sit inside this definition unless the 5641.4 exemption covers it.

B&P 5641 (unlicensed-person carve-out), official text, verified current 2026-08-15:
"This chapter shall not be deemed to prohibit any person from preparing drawings for the conceptual design and placement of tangible objects and landscape features or plans, drawings, and specifications for the selection, placement, or use of plants for a single family dwelling. Construction documents, details, or specifications for the tangible objects or landscape features, and alteration of site requiring grading and drainage plans shall be prepared by a licensed professional as required by law."
"A licensed professional as required by law" is not defined in the section.

16 CCR 832.27 (C-27 classification definition), as reproduced on CSLB's classification page:
"A landscape contractor constructs, maintains, repairs, installs, or subcontracts the development of landscape systems and facilities for public and private gardens and other areas which are designed to aesthetically, architecturally, horticulturally, or functionally improve the grounds within or surrounding a structure or a tract or plot of land. In connection therewith, a landscape contractor prepares and grades plots and areas of land for the installation of any architectural, horticultural and decorative treatment or arrangement."
The regulation assigns no design activity to the contractor; the only occurrence of "design" is the participle "designed" describing the improved areas. The C-27 design authority therefore rests entirely on 7027.5 and 5641.4, not on the regulation.

Landscape Architects Technical Committee, "Permitted Practices in California" (regulator publication, PDF, latc.ca.gov, metadata dated September 2023), verbatim:
"LANDSCAPE CONTRACTORS. Hold a C-27 (landscaping contractor) license. May design systems and facilities for work to be performed and supervised by that contractor which may include landscape construction documents and landscape drawings with specifications and details. Are exempt from the Landscape Architects Practice Act insofar as they are providing services in which they are licensed to do so."
And on unlicensed persons: "May NOT prepare construction documents, details, or specifications for tangible landscape objects or landscape features. May NOT prepare grading and drainage plans for the alteration of sites."
The document disclaims legal effect: "While every effort has been made to ensure the accuracy of this document, it does not have legal effect. Should any difference or error occur, the law will take precedence."

Negative result, stated for counsel's efficiency: no statute, regulation, published case, Attorney General opinion, or CSLB guidance was found addressing what happens when a C-27's designed work is never built, or is built by another contractor. The research located nothing resolving whether "to be performed and supervised by that contractor" is judged at the time of contracting (anticipation) or by outcome.

WHAT GMZ CURRENTLY DOES THAT THE ANSWER WOULD CHANGE: GMZ sells the design phase under its own signed agreement with no contractual commitment that GMZ will build, and clients occasionally shop the plans. Counsel's construction of "to be performed and supervised" determines whether the design agreement must recite intent that GMZ perform the work, whether it should price or restrict plan portability, and whether GMZ can market "design services" to clients who state up front they may bid the construction out.

QUESTION 2: ASSEMBLED TEXTS

B&P 7151.2 (definition of home improvement contract), official text, last amended Stats. 1991, Ch. 1160, verified current 2026-08-15:
"'Home improvement contract' means an agreement, whether oral or written, or contained in one or more documents, between a contractor and an owner or between a contractor and a tenant, regardless of the number of residence or dwelling units contained in the building in which the tenant resides, if the work is to be performed in, to, or upon the residence or dwelling unit of the tenant, for the performance of a home improvement as defined in Section 7151, and includes all labor, services, and materials to be furnished and performed thereunder."
The section's second sentence extends the definition to salesperson agreements "for the sale, installation, or furnishing of home improvement goods or services." The text is silent on design-only agreements.

B&P 7151 (definition of home improvement), official text, last amended Stats. 2021, Ch. 249 (SB 757), verified current 2026-08-15:
"'Home improvement' shall also mean the installation of home improvement goods or the furnishing of home improvement services. For purposes of this chapter, 'home improvement goods or services' means goods and services, as defined in Section 1689.5 of the Civil Code, which are bought in connection with the improvement of real property."
Section 7151 also expressly lists "landscaping" and "fences" among home improvements.

Civil Code 1689.5(d), official text, last amended Stats. 2020, Ch. 158 (AB 2471), verified current 2026-08-15:
"'Services' means work, labor and services, including, but not limited to, services furnished in connection with the repair, restoration, alteration, or improvement of residential premises, or services furnished in connection with the sale or repair of goods"
The 1689.5(d) exclusions cover attorneys, real estate professionals, securities dealers, physicians, optometrists and dentists; design professionals are not excluded. Section 1689.5(a) sets the home solicitation contract threshold at $25 or more "made at other than appropriate trade premises." Section 1689.5(f) defines senior citizen as an individual 65 years of age or older.

The definitional chain, laid out for counsel: 7151.2 (home improvement contract) incorporates 7151 (home improvement), which incorporates CIV 1689.5 services "bought in connection with the improvement of real property." A paid design fee is plausibly a service bought in connection with the improvement of real property. That final step is the researcher's inference, not stated in any source found. No statute, regulation, or published guidance expressly classifying a contractor's design-only agreement as inside or outside the home improvement contract regime was located.

WHAT GMZ CURRENTLY DOES THAT THE ANSWER WOULD CHANGE: GMZ's design agreement is currently drafted as a professional-services agreement, not on the 7159 home improvement contract form, and its retainer structure was not set with the 7159.5 downpayment cap (the lesser of $1,000 or 10 percent) in mind. If counsel concludes the chain reaches design-only agreements, or that the safe course is to assume it does, the design agreement needs the full 7159 apparatus: statutory notices, the cancellation notice block, and a deposit at or under the cap. The research's working observation, for counsel to confirm or reject: drafting to 7159 costs little and forecloses the argument.

QUESTION 3: ASSEMBLED TEXTS

B&P 7159(e)(6), official text, last amended Stats. 2025, Ch. 585 (SB 517), effective 2026-01-01; the provisions below were re-verified in the current post-SB 517 text on 2026-08-15:
"(A) The notice ... entitled 'Three-Day Right to Cancel,' or entitled 'Five-Day Right to Cancel' for contracts with a senior citizen, shall be provided to the buyer unless the contract is: (i) Negotiated at the contractor's place of business. (ii) Subject to the 'Seven-Day Right to Cancel,' as set forth in paragraph (7). (iii) Subject to licensure under the Alarm Company Act..."
Required notice text, (B)(i): "You, the buyer, have the right to cancel this contract within three business days. You may cancel by emailing, mailing, faxing, or delivering a written notice to the contractor at the contractor's place of business by midnight of the third business day after you received a signed and dated copy of the contract that includes this notice."
(B)(ii): references to "three" and "third" are changed to "five" and "fifth" for a buyer who is a senior citizen.
7159(a)(2), verbatim: the section "does not apply to service and repair contracts that are subject to Section 7159.10, if the contract for the applicable services complies with Sections 7159.10 to 7159.14, inclusive."

CSLB, "Home Improvement Contracts, Warnings and Exceptions" (consumer guidance page, cslb.ca.gov, undated, post-2020), verbatim:
"Unless the contract is negotiated at the contractor's place of business, and/or the contract price is under $25, the buyer qualifies for a three-day right to cancel. ... Starting in 2021, seniors (those 65 and older) will have five days to cancel the following transactions: home solicitation contracts, home improvement contracts, Property Assessed Clean Energy assessment contracts, service and repair contracts, and seminar sales contracts (AB 2471)."
Also on that page, verbatim: "The right to a three-day notice automatically is canceled the moment the contract is signed and the contractor begins working on a 'Service and Repair' contract."

The tension assembled for counsel: the statutory trigger in 7159(e)(6)(A) is purely locational (negotiated at the contractor's place of business or not), with no dollar threshold; CSLB's framing imports the $25 floor from CIV 1689.5's home solicitation definition. The clock in the statutory notice runs from the buyer's receipt of a signed and dated copy of the contract containing the notice, not from signature alone. Points counsel should be aware of: (a) 7159 was amended by SB 517 effective 2026-01-01; the quoted provisions were verified present in the current text, but the full scope of the SB 517 changes was not diffed, and counsel should pull the complete current section, including paragraph (7)'s Seven-Day Right to Cancel; (b) the CSLB guidance page predates SB 517 and may be stale; (c) DCA Legal Guide K-10 (dca.ca.gov/publications/legal_guides/k_10.pdf) surfaced in search as a further reconciliation source but was not fetched.

WHAT GMZ CURRENTLY DOES THAT THE ANSWER WOULD CHANGE: GMZ negotiates and signs at clients' homes, so on the statutory trigger every design and construction agreement carries the notice regardless of price. GMZ does not currently screen buyers for age 65 and over, and its Peninsula clientele makes the Five-Day variant frequently the correct one. GMZ also sometimes begins design work (site measurements, base plan) within days of signing. Counsel's answer determines: the intake step for identifying senior buyers, whether GMZ should adopt the five-day notice universally as the conservative form, the internal rule for the earliest work-start date after contract delivery, and the document-delivery practice (the countdown does not start until the client has received the signed, dated copy containing the notice, so same-day delivery of the executed copy matters).

QUESTION 4: ASSEMBLED TEXTS

The license-authority limit that the plan-license clause must respect is the same "for work to be performed and supervised by that contractor" language quoted under Question 1 (B&P 7027.5(a) and 5641.4).

B&P 5640 (misdemeanor; penalties), official text, last amended Stats. 2024, Ch. 482 (SB 1452), effective 2025-01-01, verified current 2026-08-15:
"It is a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of not less than one hundred dollars ($100) nor more than five thousand dollars ($5,000) or by imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding six months, or by both that fine and imprisonment, for a person to do any of the following without possessing a valid, unrevoked license as provided in this chapter: (a) Engage in the practice of landscape architecture. (b) Use the title or term 'landscape architect,' 'landscape architecture,' 'landscape architectural,' or any other titles, words, or abbreviations that would imply or indicate that they are a landscape architect, as defined in Section 5615."
Subdivisions (c) (use of a licensed LA's stamp) and (d) (advertising or signage suggesting licensure) extend the prohibition.

B&P 5641, quoted in full under Question 1: construction documents, details, specifications, and grading and drainage plans must be prepared by "a licensed professional as required by law." The LATC Permitted Practices document (quoted under Question 1) reads the licensed-professional universe to include C-27 contractors via 5641.4, and states the C-27's deliverables "may include landscape construction documents and landscape drawings with specifications and details."

B&P 7027.5(e), quoted under Question 1: no authority to perform work requiring a Professional Engineers Act license.

Related advertising provision, B&P 7027.1, official text, verified current 2026-08-15: "(a) It is a misdemeanor for any person to advertise for construction or work of improvement covered by this chapter unless that person holds a valid license under this chapter in the classification so advertised... (c) A violation of this section is punishable by a fine of not less than seven hundred dollars ($700) and not more than one thousand dollars ($1,000)..." The advertising definition was verified to include "airwave or any electronic transmission," which reaches the company website.

Drafting questions assembled for counsel, flowing from these texts: (a) whether the plan license should be expressly conditioned, for example a license to use the plans limited to construction performed and supervised by GMZ, with a separate conversation if the client goes elsewhere; (b) whether an unconditional transfer of construction-ready documents to a client who builds with another contractor retroactively undermines the 7027.5/5641.4 exemption for the preparation of those documents; (c) whether tiering the deliverables helps, since B&P 5641 permits anyone to prepare conceptual drawings and plant-selection plans for a single family dwelling, so a conceptual-tier package may be portable without licensing questions while the construction-document tier is not; (d) what disclaimer wording keeps every document clear of the protected titles, given that "landscape architectural" itself is a prohibited term; (e) whether the agreement should state that engineering items (for example engineered retaining walls) are excluded and referred out, per 7027.5(e).

WHAT GMZ CURRENTLY DOES THAT THE ANSWER WOULD CHANGE: the current design agreement transfers the plan set to the client on final payment without a limited-license clause, GMZ marketing describes the offering as "landscape design," and the plan sheets carry no scope disclaimer. Counsel's language would be dropped directly into the agreement's intellectual-property section, the plan title block, and the website services page.

QUESTION 5: ASSEMBLED TEXTS

B&P 7159.10(a)(1), official text, last amended Stats. 2020, Ch. 158 (AB 2471), verified current 2026-08-15. A service and repair contract escaping full 7159 formalities must satisfy all four conditions:
"(A) The contract amount is seven hundred fifty dollars ($750) or less. (B) The prospective buyer initiated contact with the contractor to request the work. (C) The contractor does not sell the buyer goods or services beyond those reasonably necessary to take care of the particular problem that caused the buyer to contact the contractor. (D) No payment is due, or accepted by the contractor, until the work is completed."
Condition (D) makes the service-and-repair route incompatible with any advance payment. Work above $750, or contractor-solicited work, falls back into full 7159 territory. The interaction provision is 7159(a)(2), quoted under Question 3: 7159 does not apply to service and repair contracts subject to 7159.10 if the contract complies with 7159.10 through 7159.14 inclusive. CSLB's guidance page adds, verbatim: "The right to a three-day notice automatically is canceled the moment the contract is signed and the contractor begins working on a 'Service and Repair' contract."

Also assembled here because the maintenance accounts auto-renew, B&P 17602 (automatic renewal law), official text, last amended Stats. 2024, Ch. 515 (AB 2863), effective 2025-01-01, applying to contracts entered into, amended, or extended on or after July 1, 2025 (chaptered bill text, verbatim: "The amendments made to this section by the act adding this subdivision shall only apply to a contract entered into, amended, or extended under this article on or after July 1, 2025."):
Renewal reminder for terms of one year or longer, verbatim timing phrase: "at least 15 days and not more than 45 days before the automatic renewal offer or continuous service offer renews."
Material-change notice, verbatim: "clear and conspicuous notice of the material change and provide information regarding how to cancel in a manner that is capable of being retained by the consumer."
Online cancellation, verbatim, applicable when the consumer accepted the offer online: "Allow a consumer to terminate the automatic renewal or continuous service exclusively online, at will, and without engaging any further steps that obstruct or delay the consumer's ability to terminate."
Because each renewal is an extension, legacy maintenance agreements are pulled into the amended regime as they roll over after July 1, 2025.

The questions inside the question, for counsel: (a) is a recurring maintenance agreement (mowing, pruning, irrigation checks at a monthly rate) a "home improvement contract" at all, given 7151's inclusion of "landscaping" and the 16 CCR 832.27 classification text placing "maintains, repairs" squarely in the C-27 classification; (b) if it is, is the contract amount measured per visit, per month, or per term for the $750 line; (c) can GMZ paper routine ad-hoc repairs under the service-and-repair form given monthly billing practices, since condition (D) forbids accepting payment before completion and condition (B) requires buyer-initiated contact, which a technician noticing a broken valve on a scheduled visit arguably is not; (d) does a 7159.10-compliant contract extinguish the cancellation right on commencement as CSLB's page states.

WHAT GMZ CURRENTLY DOES THAT THE ANSWER WOULD CHANGE: maintenance accounts run on a simple recurring agreement with monthly billing, ad-hoc repairs are performed on verbal approval and added to the monthly invoice (which violates 7159.10(a)(1)(D) if that form is the one that should govern), and renewal notices are informal. Counsel's answer sets: the contract form for the maintenance line, an internal $750 tripwire and approval path for ad-hoc work, whether repair work must be invoiced only on completion, and the 15-to-45-day renewal notice calendar with any price change stated in it.

WHAT THE RESEARCH DID NOT FIND (SO COUNSEL DOES NOT SEARCH FOR IT DURING THE HOUR)

1. No case law, AG opinion, or CSLB/LATC guidance on design-only engagements by a C-27 where construction never follows or goes to another builder. The LATC Permitted Practices document is the closest regulator statement and does not address it.
2. No authority expressly classifying a contractor's design-only agreement as inside or outside 7151.2. The chain argument under Question 2 is assembled from the texts, not from any source stating it.
3. The full effect of SB 517 (2025) on B&P 7159 was not diffed; only the quoted provisions were re-verified in the current text.
4. DCA Legal Guide K-10 was identified but not retrieved.
5. Whether a pre-agreed CPI escalation formula in an auto-renewing consumer contract is a "material change" under 17602 is unsettled in the sources found; stating each year's computed dollar amount in the pre-renewal notice moots the question in practice.

SOURCE LIST (ALL PUBLIC)

B&P 7027.5, 5641.4, 5615, 5640, 5641, 7151, 7151.2, 7159, 7159.10, 17602 and Civil Code 1689.5: official texts at leginfo.legislature.ca.gov. 16 CCR 832.27: as reproduced on CSLB's C-27 classification page. LATC, Permitted Practices in California: latc.ca.gov/docs/misc/permitted_practices_in_california.pdf. CSLB, Home Improvement Contracts, Warnings and Exceptions: cslb.ca.gov consumer pages. AB 2863 chaptered text: leginfo.legislature.ca.gov. B&P 7027.1 and 7027.3 (license-number fraud; verified but ancillary): leginfo.legislature.ca.gov.

DOCUMENTS THE OWNER SHOULD BRING TO THE MEETING

The current design agreement template; the current maintenance agreement and a sample monthly invoice showing how ad-hoc repairs are billed; one recent executed design agreement (client identifiers redacted); the website services page text; the standard proposal cover letter. Counsel marks up against the questions above; nothing further should need to be looked up.

Whether a design-only agreement is a home improvement contract under the 7151.2/7151/CIV 1689.5 chain; the chain is assembled, not sourced
Full diff of SB 517's 2026 amendments to B&P 7159, including any changes to paragraph (7)'s Seven-Day Right to Cancel
DCA Legal Guide K-10 identified but not retrieved; may bear on the cancellation-trigger reconciliation
Whether the $750 in 7159.10 is measured per visit, per month, or per term for a recurring maintenance account
Whether a pre-agreed escalation formula is a 'material change' under B&P 17602 or whether stating the computed price in the annual notice suffices

products.title: Maintenance Renewal and Escalator Design
products.body:
RECOMMENDATION: MAINTENANCE RENEWAL AND PRICE ESCALATION DESIGN
For GMZ Landscaping maintenance agreements. Prepared 2026-08-15. All dollar figures in the worked example are placeholders, not GMZ prices.

SUMMARY OF THE RECOMMENDATION
Renew every maintenance account on January 1. Escalate automatically each renewal by the June-over-June change in the San Francisco area consumer price index plus a fixed add-on, with two floors: the price never goes down, and the increase is never smaller than the state minimum wage step certified for that January. Send one notice per account each fall, in the legally required 15 to 45 day window, stating the computed new dollar price and how to cancel.

WHICH INDEX TO REFERENCE
Name the exact series, not a nickname. The clause should cite: BLS series CUURS49BSA0, Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U), San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward, all items, not seasonally adjusted; June index compared with the prior June.

Why this one:
1. It is the local index a client will accept. Its current 12-month change is 3.8 percent (June 2026 index 369.913 versus 356.460 in June 2025), confirmed in the BLS San Francisco release.
2. Its coverage includes San Mateo County, so it covers most of GMZ's towns. BLS publishes nothing finer for San Mateo County alone. Note it does not cover Santa Clara County (Palo Alto, Los Altos), which is a known imperfection, not a fixable one.
3. June is a month that actually exists for this index. The SF index is published only for even months (February, April, June, August, October, December), roughly six weeks after the fact. A clause naming an odd month can never be satisfied. The Los Gatos-Brightview contract shows the failure mode twice: it names a "San Francisco-Oakland-San Jose" index area that no longer matches any BLS title, and calls for "the CPI published on December 31," which does not exist. Fairfield's landscape maintenance contract, by contrast, pegs to the June SF print; that is the pattern to copy.
4. June lines up with the state's own machinery. The minimum wage formula in Labor Code 1182.12(c) averages CPI-W over July 1 to June 30 and must be calculated by August 1. So by early August, GMZ knows both the June CPI change and the certified January wage step, months before renewal notices go out.

Required fallback language: BLS publication can simply fail. The October 2025 observation of this very series is footnoted "Data unavailable due to the 2025 lapse in appropriations." The clause should say that if the June index is not published by September 30, the most recent published index of the same series is used, and if BLS discontinues or renames the series, the successor series or the U.S. city average CPI-U applies.

WHY PLAIN LOCAL CPI UNDERPRICES THIS TRADE
Three numbers, all current:
1. Local all-items CPI: +3.8 percent (12 months ending June 2026).
2. The trade's own price index, BLS series CUUR0000SEHP02, Gardening and lawncare services, U.S. city average: +12.3 percent over the same style of window (July 2026 index 344.925 versus 307.218 in July 2025).
3. The certified state minimum wage step for January 1, 2027: +2.99 percent ($16.90 to $17.40).

The gap between line 1 and line 2 is the problem. What clients pay for lawn and garden service nationally is rising at more than three times the local all-items rate. And the statutory wage floor understates GMZ's real labor market: May 2025 OEWS data for the SF metro puts the median landscaping worker at $23.10 per hour, about 37 percent above the state minimum, with working supervisors at a $37.02 median. Wage competition, not the minimum wage, sets GMZ's labor cost, and all-items CPI (rent, gasoline, groceries) tracks neither.

So a plain "adjusts by local CPI" clause locks in roughly 3.8 percent this year while the trade's cost environment moved by double digits. Compounded over a few renewals, that is how a maintenance account quietly goes underwater.

THE CORRECTED FORM
Three candidate corrections, and the recommendation:

1. Floor only: local CPI, but never less than a stated percentage. Simple, but in a high-inflation trade year the floor does nothing; it only protects against low-CPI years.
2. Trade-index reference: peg directly to the gardening and lawncare series. Honest, but unusable as the sole peg. It is national, volatile, and would have demanded 12.3 percent this year, which Peninsula clients would likely reject. Keep it as the internal justification, not the contract peg.
3. Index-plus with floors (recommended): local CPI plus a fixed add-on, with a floor at the minimum wage step and an upward-only ratchet.

Recommended clause architecture, in plain terms:
- Each January 1, the monthly price adjusts by the percentage change in the named June index over the prior June, plus [1.5] percentage points (add-on size is Xavier's call, see decisions).
- The increase is never less than the minimum wage increase percentage certified by the Director of Finance for that January 1 (2.99 percent for 2027).
- The price never decreases; if the formula yields a negative number, the price holds. This upward-only floor is client-tested language: the Los Gatos public contract uses exactly this ratchet ("If the CPI indicates a downward adjustment, compensation will remain at the base amount").
- Optional cap: a stated maximum (for example 6 percent) makes the clause easier to sell and mirrors the state's own lesser-of-3.5-percent cap design in Labor Code 1182.12(c), which also supplies a copyable pattern for rounding and announcement timing.

ALIGNING RENEWAL WITH THE JANUARY WAGE STEP
Every certified minimum wage change takes effect January 1, announced by August 1. Renewing all accounts on January 1 means each year's price adjusts in the same month the labor floor steps, instead of eating a wage increase mid-term. The calendar works out cleanly:
- Mid-July: June SF CPI publishes.
- By August 1: Department of Finance certifies the January wage step (done July 31, 2026 for the 2027 step).
- Early August: GMZ computes every account's new price. All inputs are known.
- November 17 to December 17: renewal notices go out (the legal window for a January 1 renewal).
- January 1: new price takes effect.
Accounts currently renewing on other anniversaries should be migrated to January 1 at their next renewal, using a short prorated stub period if needed.

WHAT CALIFORNIA'S AUTOMATIC RENEWAL LAW REQUIRES
These accounts are consumer contracts that renew automatically, so Business and Professions Code 17602 (as amended by AB 2863) governs. Four requirements, quoted:

1. Annual reminder notice, for contracts with an initial term of one year or longer, sent "at least 15 days and not more than 45 days before the automatic renewal offer or continuous service offer renews," disclosing the service, the renewal frequency and charges, and how to cancel.

2. Notice before a price change. Before a material change to the terms, the business must give "clear and conspicuous notice of the material change and provide information regarding how to cancel in a manner that is capable of being retained by the consumer." Whether a pre-agreed formula increase counts as a material change is unsettled; the safe practice is to never apply the escalator silently. State the computed new dollar amount in the fall notice every year, which moots the question. One notice can lawfully carry both the renewal reminder and the new price.

3. Cancellation channel. If a consumer accepted the agreement online, GMZ must "Allow a consumer to terminate the automatic renewal or continuous service exclusively online, at will, and without engaging any further steps that obstruct or delay the consumer's ability to terminate," including "A prominently located direct link or button." If GMZ signs on paper or by emailed signature, the online-exclusive duty is not triggered, but the agreement must still name an easy cancellation channel such as a phone number or email address. Practical implication: keep maintenance signup off any website checkout flow unless GMZ is prepared to build online cancellation.

4. No grandfathering. AB 2863 provides: "The amendments made to this section by the act adding this subdivision shall only apply to a contract entered into, amended, or extended under this article on or after July 1, 2025." A renewal is an extension, so every one of the roughly two dozen existing accounts is pulled into the amended rules at its next rollover. The paperwork should be updated now, not only for new clients.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A HYPOTHETICAL $1,000 PER MONTH ACCOUNT
Placeholder amount only. Assume the recommended clause: June-over-June CUURS49BSA0 change plus 1.5 points, floored at the certified wage step, upward-only, rounded to the nearest dollar.

Year 1 (renewal January 1, 2027):
- June 2026 index change: +3.8 percent.
- Formula: 3.8 + 1.5 = 5.3 percent.
- Floor check: certified wage step is 2.99 percent; 5.3 is higher, so 5.3 applies.
- New price: $1,000 x 1.053 = $1,053 per month.
- Notice sent between November 17 and December 17, 2026, stating $1,053, the January 1 date, and how to cancel.
- Comparison: plain CPI alone gives $1,038; the trade index alone would demand $1,123, which is the increase a client would refuse.

Year 2 (renewal January 1, 2028), assuming inflation cools:
- Assume June 2027 index change is +2.0 percent and the certified wage step is +3.1 percent (both hypothetical).
- Formula: 2.0 + 1.5 = 3.5 percent. Floor check: 3.5 exceeds 3.1, so 3.5 applies.
- New price: $1,053 x 1.035 = $1,090 per month.

Stress cases the clause handles:
- Negative CPI year: formula could go negative; the price holds at the prior amount.
- Wage step outruns CPI: if CPI-plus computes below the certified step (say CPI +1.0 gives 2.5 percent against a 3.4 percent wage step), the wage-step floor governs.
- Missing index: if the June print never publishes (as happened October 2025), the fallback uses the most recent published print.

Two-year effect on the placeholder account: $1,000 to $1,090, about 9 percent cumulative, against roughly 7.7 percent under plain CPI in the same scenario, communicated in two predictable fall notices with an exit door each time.

DECISIONS XAVIER STILL HAS TO MAKE
1. The add-on size: how many points above local CPI (the example uses 1.5; anywhere in 1 to 2 is defensible given the 3.8 versus 12.3 gap), and whether to include a cap, and at what level.
2. Whether to migrate all existing accounts to a January 1 renewal at next rollover, and how to price the stub months.
3. The cancellation channel the agreement names (phone, email, or both), and whether maintenance signup will ever move online, which would trigger the online-exclusive cancellation duty.
4. Whether commercial or HOA accounts, if GMZ ever takes them, get the same clause; the automatic renewal law would not govern those, so the notice mechanics could differ.
5. Whether small ad-hoc repairs on maintenance accounts use the service-and-repair contract form (only valid at $750 or less, client-initiated, no payment until complete).
6. Counsel review of the final clause and notice text before the first fall notice cycle, including the unsettled material-change question.
7. Whether to check the Peninsula cities' own minimum wage ordinances, which can exceed the state floor and were not pulled in this study.
openItems: Peninsula city minimum wage ordinances above the state floor were not researched; several GMZ towns may have their own, which would move the wage-step floor for crews working there.
Whether a pre-agreed escalation formula is a 'material change' under B&P 17602 is legally unsettled; the recommended annual dollar-amount notice sidesteps rather than resolves it.
The SF-Oakland-Hayward index excludes Santa Clara County, so Palo Alto and Los Altos accounts escalate on an index that does not technically cover them; no finer BLS index exists.
Exact add-on size, cap level, and rounding convention are business decisions, not research questions.
Year 2 of the worked example uses hypothetical CPI and wage-step values, since neither is published yet.
Treatment of any future commercial or HOA maintenance accounts, which sit outside the consumer automatic renewal law.

WATER REBATE QUICK REFERENCE, GMZ PENINSULA TOWNS
Internal one-page sales reference. All figures below were checked on 2026-08-15.

READ THIS BEFORE QUOTING ANY NUMBER
Rebate amounts change, often at the fiscal year, and every figure on this page carries the date it was checked. This document must never be used to state a rebate as certain. Eligibility, the final amount, and approval are always the water agency's call, never GMZ's. Before a dollar figure goes into any proposal or conversation, re-check the agency page that week.

The one rule that applies everywhere: the client must apply and hold the agency's written go-ahead (a Notice to Proceed) before any lawn is removed. Turf removed early is permanently ineligible. GMZ sequences every job so demolition day comes after the Notice to Proceed arrives.

TOWN BY TOWN

REDWOOD CITY
Rate: $2.00 per sq ft (checked 2026-08-15). Program: Lawn Be Gone!, run through the regional water conservation program for San Mateo County agencies. Cap: not stated on the program page; confirm with the agency. Key condition: submit the application and receive a Notice to Proceed from the water provider before removing any lawn. Apply through: bayareaconservation.org/rebates/lawn. Caution: the program page is undated and its linked documents reference older fiscal years, so confirm the current-year rate with the agency before quoting.

MENLO PARK
Rate: $3.00 per sq ft (checked 2026-08-15). Same program, same Notice to Proceed rule, same application page and same currency caution as Redwood City. Cap not stated on the page.

HILLSBOROUGH
Rate: $1.00 per sq ft (checked 2026-08-15). Same program, same Notice to Proceed rule, same application page and same currency caution. Cap not stated on the page.

PALO ALTO AND LOS ALTOS
Rate: $2.00 per sq ft through the Santa Clara County water district's Landscape Rebate Program (checked 2026-08-15). Cap: $3,000 default for single-family residential; a $6,000 cost-share cap applies in some areas. Key conditions: a completed pre-inspection (the lawn must still be in place) and a written Notice to Proceed before any lawn removal or any material purchase; projects started early are permanently ineligible. Funding is stated to last until June 30, 2027 or until depleted. Apply through: valleywater.org/saving-water/rebates-surveys/landscape-rebates. Note: Palo Alto does not appear on the San Mateo County program's participating-agency list, so the county district program is the confirmed route; also confirm with the client's own water utility whether a separate city program applies.

SAN CARLOS AND BELMONT
Check with your water supplier. The regional program page lists Mid-Peninsula Water District at $4.00 per sq ft (checked 2026-08-15), but whether that district serves a given San Carlos or Belmont address was not confirmed from an agency page. Confirm the client's supplier first; if it is Mid-Peninsula Water District, the $4.00 rate and the Notice to Proceed rule apply through bayareaconservation.org/rebates/lawn.

ATHERTON, WOODSIDE AND PORTOLA VALLEY
Check with your water supplier. No agency page confirmed a town-specific rebate rate for these towns. Many addresses here are served by an investor-owned water utility whose lawn-to-garden program is confirmed to exist, with these confirmed terms (checked 2026-08-15): pre-approval is required before the project begins, at least 3 approved plants per 100 sq ft converted, and artificial turf does not qualify. That utility does not publish its per-square-foot rate on its public page; the rate is visible only inside the customer's own conservation account. The honest move: have the client open their conservation account during the design phase so the real number is on the table before pricing. Program page: calwater.com/conservation-rebates.

EXTRAS
A $300 flat rain-garden rebate is listed on the regional San Mateo County program page where the agency participates (checked 2026-08-15); confirm participation per agency.

CONDITIONS THAT SHOW UP ACROSS PROGRAMS
1. Application approved and written Notice to Proceed in hand before removal. Every confirmed program requires this.
2. Pre-inspection with the lawn still alive and in place (confirmed for the Santa Clara County district program). Do not let a client stop watering to "kill it off early" before approval.
3. Plant coverage minimums (confirmed at 3 approved plants per 100 sq ft for the investor-owned utility). Expect similar elsewhere.
4. Artificial turf does not qualify (confirmed for the investor-owned utility; assume the same elsewhere until an agency page says otherwise).

WHAT TO SAY TO A CLIENT (adapt as needed, keep the hedges)
Most water suppliers in our area will actually pay you to take out a thirsty lawn and replace it with a garden suited to our climate. The amount depends on who supplies your water, and the rules matter: your application has to be approved, and you need the agency's written go-ahead in hand, before a single square foot of lawn comes out. We build that step into the project schedule so nothing gets forfeited. The rebate is always the agency's decision, not ours, so we treat it as a welcome bonus rather than a promise, and we help you confirm the current amount for your address before we ever set a demolition date.

OPERATING NOTES FOR THE GMZ TEAM
Sequence every rebate job: design, application, pre-inspection if required, Notice to Proceed received, then demo. Put the Notice to Proceed date on the schedule as a gate, not a hope. Never write a rebate amount into a proposal as a credit against GMZ's price; it is the agency's money paid on the agency's terms. Re-verify each figure on this page before quoting it; the check date on every number is 2026-08-15.

Which of Atherton, Woodside and Portola Valley fall inside Cal Water's Bear Gulch district was not verified from a primary source, so those three towns are listed as check-with-your-supplier.
